chapters.title: The Noble Bachelor
paragraphs: Lord St. Simon’s marriage and its curious ending have long since lost their interest for the distinguished circles in which the unfortunate bridegroom moves. New scandals, with more tempting details, have drawn the gossips away from that drama of four years ago. Yet I have reason to believe the public has never heard the full facts. Since my friend Sherlock Holmes played a considerable part in explaining them, I feel that no account of his life would be complete without a brief description of this remarkable affair.

It was a few weeks before my own marriage, while I still shared Holmes’s rooms in Baker Street. Returning from an afternoon walk, he found a letter waiting on the table. I had stayed inside all day: the weather had suddenly turned wet, with strong autumn winds, and the jezail bullet lodged in one of my limbs—a souvenir of Afghanistan—ached steadily. Seated in one armchair with my legs resting on another, I had surrounded myself with newspapers. At last, thoroughly saturated with the day’s news, I threw them aside and lay listlessly studying the large crest and monogram on the envelope. I wondered idly which noble correspondent had written to my friend.
“A very fashionable letter awaits you,” I said as he entered. “This morning’s letters, if I remember correctly, came from a fishmonger and a customs officer.”

“Yes, variety certainly lends my correspondence its charm,” he replied, smiling. “The humbler writers are usually more interesting. This looks like one of those tiresome social invitations that force a man either to be bored or to tell a lie.”
He opened the sealed envelope and scanned the letter.
“Ah, perhaps there is something interesting here after all.”
“Not a social invitation?”
“No, decidedly professional business.”
“And a nobleman as client?”
“One of the highest-ranking in England.”
“My dear fellow, you have my congratulations.”

“I assure you quite sincerely, Watson, that a client’s rank matters less to me than the interest of his problem. This new enquiry may offer that as well, however. You have been following all the newspapers closely lately, have you not?”
“So it would appear,” I said ruefully, indicating a large bundle in the corner. “There has been nothing else to occupy me.”

“Good. You may be able to bring me up to date. I read only crime reports and the personal notices; the latter are always revealing. If you have followed recent events so closely, you must know about Lord St. Simon’s wedding?”
“Indeed, I read about it with great interest.”

“Excellent. This letter is from Lord St. Simon himself. I shall read the letter aloud to you. In exchange, look through your newspapers and find everything relevant to the affair. Here is what he writes:

“‘Dear Mr. Sherlock Holmes,—Lord Backwater assures me that I can rely completely on your judgement and discretion. I have therefore decided to visit you for advice about the deeply distressing events surrounding my wedding. Mr. Lestrade of Scotland Yard is already investigating. He assures me that he has no objection to your cooperation and believes it might even be helpful. I shall call at four this afternoon. If you have another engagement, I trust you will postpone it, as this matter is of the utmost importance. Yours faithfully,
“‘ROBERT ST. SIMON.’
“The letter is dated from Grosvenor Mansions and written with a quill,” Holmes observed as he folded it. “His lordship also had the misfortune to smear ink on the outside of his right little finger.”
“He says four o’clock. It is three now, so he should arrive in an hour.”

“That gives me just enough time, with your help, to understand the affair. Find the reports and arrange them by date while I look up our client.” He took a red volume from the reference books beside the mantelpiece. “Here he is,” he said, sitting and opening it on his knee. “‘Lord Robert Walsingham de Vere St. Simon, second son of the Duke of Balmoral.’ Hmm! ‘Arms: Azure, three caltrops in chief over a fess sable. Born in 1846.’ Forty-one: rather mature for a bridegroom. Under-Secretary for the colonies in a recent government. His father, the Duke, formerly Secretary for Foreign Affairs. Direct descent from the Plantagenets, and Tudor blood on the female side. Well, none of this tells us much. I must look to you for something more substantial, Watson.”

“I have little trouble finding the reports I want,” I replied. “The events are quite recent, and they struck me as extraordinary. I hesitated to mention them to you because I knew you had another enquiry under way and disliked unrelated matters intruding.”
“Ah, the little puzzle of the Grosvenor Square furniture van. That is entirely settled, though it was obvious from the outset. Please give me what you have found in the newspapers.”

“Here is the earliest notice, in the _Morning Post_’s personal column. It is dated several weeks ago: ‘A marriage has been arranged and, if reports are accurate, will shortly take place between Lord Robert St. Simon, second son of the Duke of Balmoral, and Miss Hatty Doran, only daughter of Aloysius Doran, Esq., of San Francisco, California, U.S.A.’ That is the entire announcement.”
“Brief and direct,” Holmes remarked, extending his long, thin legs towards the fire.

“A society paper that same week supplied more detail. Ah, here: ‘We may soon hear demands for protection in the marriage market, since free trade seems to put the home product at a serious disadvantage. One by one, Britain’s great aristocratic houses are falling under the management of our beautiful cousins across the Atlantic. Last week brought another notable addition to the prizes won by these charming invaders. Lord St. Simon, resistant for over twenty years to the little god’s arrows, has formally announced his forthcoming marriage to Miss Hatty Doran, the fascinating daughter of a Californian millionaire. Miss Doran’s graceful figure and striking features attracted considerable attention at the Westbury House festivities. An only child, she is said to bring a dowry well above six figures, with further prospects to come. The Duke of Balmoral’s sale of pictures in recent years is an open secret, while Lord St. Simon owns nothing beyond the small Birchmoor estate. Clearly the Californian heiress is not the only person to benefit from an alliance allowing her the easy and familiar change from a republican lady into a British peeress.’”
“Is there more?” Holmes asked, yawning.

“Yes, a good deal. Then there is another notice in the _Morning Post_ which says the wedding will be entirely private, at St. George’s, Hanover Square, with only six close friends invited. Afterwards the party will return to the furnished house Mr. Aloysius Doran has rented at Lancaster Gate. Two days later—last Wednesday—a brief announcement states that the wedding has taken place and the honeymoon will be spent at Lord Backwater’s estate near Petersfield. Those are all the reports preceding the bride’s disappearance.”
“Her what?” Holmes asked, suddenly alert.
“The lady disappeared completely.”
“When did this happen?”
“During the wedding breakfast.”
“Indeed! This is more interesting than I had expected. Quite dramatic, in fact.”
“Yes. I thought it distinctly out of the ordinary.”
“Brides often disappear before the ceremony, sometimes during the honeymoon. But I remember nothing quite so immediate. Please give me the details.”
“I must warn you, they are very incomplete.”
“Perhaps we can fill the gaps.”
“The details, such as they are, appear in one article in yesterday’s morning paper. I shall read it. The heading is ‘Strange Incident at a Society Wedding’:

“‘Lord Robert St. Simon’s family is deeply alarmed by the strange and distressing events connected with his wedding. As yesterday’s newspapers briefly reported, the ceremony took place the preceding morning. Only now, however, have we been able to confirm the unusual rumours that have circulated so persistently. Despite the attempts of friends to hush the whole affair up, so much public attention has now been drawn to the matter that pretending to ignore what everyone is talking about can serve no useful purpose.

“‘The ceremony at St. George’s, Hanover Square, was very private. Present were only the bride’s father, Mr. Aloysius Doran; the Duchess of Balmoral; Lord Backwater; Lord Eustace and Lady Clara St. Simon, the bridegroom’s younger brother and sister; and Lady Alicia Whittington. Afterwards they all went to Mr. Doran’s house at Lancaster Gate, where breakfast awaited them. Some disturbance apparently arose when an unidentified woman tried to follow the bridal party into the house, declaring that she had a claim on Lord St. Simon. After a prolonged and embarrassing scene, the butler and footman removed her. Fortunately the bride had gone inside before this unpleasant interruption. She joined the company at breakfast, then complained of suddenly feeling unwell and went upstairs. Her lengthy absence attracted comment, and her father followed. Her maid said she had entered her room only briefly, picked up an ulster and bonnet, and hurried downstairs to the passage. One of the footmen declared that he had seen a woman leave the house dressed in just that manner but had not believed it was his mistress, whom he supposed to be with the guests. On discovering her disappearance, Mr. Doran and the bridegroom immediately contacted the police. Energetic enquiries are proceeding and will probably bring a rapid explanation of this extraordinary affair. By late last night, however, no news of the missing lady’s whereabouts had emerged. Foul play is rumoured. The police are reportedly holding the woman responsible for the earlier disturbance, believing that jealousy or some other motive may have led her to take part in the bride’s strange disappearance.’”
“Is that everything?”
“There is just one other small item, though a suggestive one, in another morning paper.”
“And what is it?”

“Miss Flora Millar, who was responsible for the disturbance, has indeed been arrested. She was formerly a _danseuse_ at the Allegro and has known the bridegroom for several years. There are no further details. You now know the entire case, at least as the newspapers present it.”

“And a most interesting case it appears to be. I would not have missed it for anything. But there is the bell, Watson. The clock shows a few minutes after four, so that will surely be our noble client. Do not think of leaving: I much prefer having a witness, if only to check my own recollection.”

“Lord Robert St. Simon,” our page announced, opening the door. A gentleman entered with a pleasant, cultivated face: pale, high-nosed, perhaps a little peevish around the mouth, and with the steady, open gaze of someone always accustomed to command and receive obedience. His movements were brisk, yet he looked older than he should, stooping slightly forward and bending a little at the knees as he walked. When he removed his sharply curled-brimmed hat, his hair proved grey at the edges and thin on top. His clothes were chosen with almost foppish care: high collar, black frock-coat, white waistcoat, yellow gloves, patent-leather shoes, and pale gaiters. He advanced slowly, looking from side to side and swinging the cord of his gold eyeglasses in his right hand.
“Good afternoon, Lord St. Simon,” Holmes said, rising and bowing. “Please take the wicker chair. This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson. Come closer to the fire, and let us discuss the affair.”

“A deeply painful affair, as you can imagine, Mr. Holmes. I am wounded to the quick. I understand you have handled delicate matters of this sort before, although presumably not involving quite the same social class.”
“No. This is a step down.”
“I beg your pardon?”
“My previous client in such a case was a king.”
“Really! I had no idea. Which king was that?”
“The King of Scandinavia.”
“What! Had his wife disappeared?”
“You will appreciate,” Holmes replied smoothly, “that I observe the same discretion about other clients’ affairs that I promise you concerning yours.”
“Naturally! Quite right, quite right! I beg your pardon. In my own case, I shall gladly supply anything that may help you reach an opinion.”
“Thank you. I have learned everything reported in the newspapers, but nothing beyond that. May I assume those reports are accurate—this article about the bride’s disappearance, for instance?”
Lord St. Simon read it. “Yes, it is accurate as far as it goes.”
“It needs considerable additions before anyone can judge the matter. Direct questions may be the quickest way to establish the facts.”
“Please ask them.”
“When did you first meet Miss Hatty Doran?”
“A year ago, in San Francisco.”
“Were you travelling in the United States?”
“Yes.”
“Did you become engaged at that time?”
“No.”
“But you were friendly with one another?”
“I enjoyed her company, and she could see that I enjoyed it.”
“Her father is very wealthy?”
“People say he is the richest man on the Pacific slope.”
“How did he acquire his fortune?”
“Mining. A few years ago he had nothing. Then he found gold, invested the proceeds, and rose rapidly.”
“What is your own impression of the young lady’s—your wife’s character?”

The nobleman swung his eyeglasses faster and looked into the fire. “You see, Mr. Holmes, she was twenty before her father became wealthy. Until then she ran freely about a mining camp and roamed the woods and mountains. Nature, rather than a schoolmaster, educated her. In England we would call her a tomboy: strong-willed, wild, independent, and bound by no traditions. She is impetuous—almost volcanic, I might say. She decides quickly and acts without fear. Yet I would never have bestowed on her the name I am honoured to bear”—he gave a dignified little cough—“unless I believed her fundamentally noble. I believe that she is capable of heroic self-sacrifice, and I believe any kind of dishonourable act would disgust her.”
“Do you have a photograph of her?”

“I brought this.” He opened a locket to reveal the full face of a beautiful woman. It was an ivory miniature, not a photograph. The artist had captured the brilliance of her black hair, her large dark eyes, and her exquisite mouth. Holmes studied it intently for some time before closing the locket and returning it to Lord St. Simon.
“Then she came to London, and you met again?”
“Yes. Her father brought her for the latest London season. We met several times, became engaged, and have now married.”
“She brought a substantial dowry, I understand?”
“A reasonable one. Nothing beyond what is customary in my family.”
“Which naturally remains yours, now that the marriage is a _fait accompli_?”
“I have really made no enquiries about that.”
“Naturally. Did you see Miss Doran the day before the wedding?”
“Yes.”
“Was she in cheerful spirits?”
“Never more so. She talked continually about our future life together.”
“Indeed! Most interesting. And on the wedding morning itself?”
“As cheerful as she could possibly be—at least until the ceremony was over.”
“Did you notice a change in her afterwards?”
“To tell the truth, I then saw the first indication that her temper might be rather sharp. But the incident was too insignificant to mention and cannot possibly concern this case.”
“Nevertheless, please tell us about it.”

“It was childish. On our way to the vestry, she dropped her bouquet. She was passing the front pew, and the flowers fell inside it. There was a moment’s delay before a gentleman sitting there handed them back. They seemed none the worse for the fall. Yet when I spoke to her about it, she answered sharply. In the carriage on our way home she seemed absurdly upset by such a trifling cause.”
“Indeed! A man was sitting in the pew, you say. Were members of the public present?”
“Yes. One cannot keep them out while the church is open.”
“He was not a friend of your wife’s?”
“No, no. I call him a gentleman merely out of politeness. He was quite a common-looking person. I scarcely noticed him. Really, though, I think we are straying rather far from the point.”
“So Lady St. Simon came home less cheerful than when she left for the wedding. What did she do on returning to her father’s house?”
“I noticed her talking to her maid.”
“Who is this maid?”
“Her name is Alice. She is American and accompanied her from California.”
“A trusted confidante?”
“Rather too much of one. It seemed to me that her mistress allowed her to take considerable liberties. Naturally, though, Americans take a different view of such things.”
“How long did their conversation last?”
“A few minutes. I had other things to attend to.”
“Did you happen to hear any of it?”
“Lady St. Simon mentioned ‘jumping a claim’. She often used expressions of that sort. I have no idea what she meant.”
“American slang can be remarkably expressive. What did your wife do after speaking with her maid?”
“She went into the breakfast-room.”
“Holding your arm?”
“No, by herself. She was very independent about such little things. About ten minutes after we sat down, she rose abruptly, murmured an apology, and left. She did not return.”
“But Alice states, I understand, that she went upstairs, put a long ulster over her wedding dress, added a bonnet, and left the house.”
“Exactly. Later she was seen entering Hyde Park with Flora Millar, who is now under arrest and had already caused a disturbance at Mr. Doran’s that morning.”
“Yes. I should like some details about this woman and your connection with her.”

Lord St. Simon shrugged and lifted his eyebrows. “We have been friends for years—_very_ close friends, I might say. She formerly worked at the Allegro. I have not treated her ungenerously at all, and she had no legitimate complaint, but you know how women are, Mr. Holmes. Flora was a dear little creature, intensely attached to me and extremely hot-headed. When she heard of my engagement, she sent dreadful letters. In fact, I arranged so quiet a wedding because I feared a scene in church. She arrived at Mr. Doran’s just after we returned and tried to force her way inside, abusing and even threatening my wife. I had anticipated trouble and stationed two plain-clothes policemen there. Those men soon pushed her out of the house again. When she saw that she could gain nothing by making a disturbance, she became quiet.”
“Did your wife hear this scene?”
“Thankfully, no. She heard nothing of it.”
“Yet afterwards she was seen walking with the same woman?”
“Yes. Mr. Lestrade considers that very significant. The theory is that Flora lured my wife outside and led her into some dreadful trap.”
“That is certainly a possible explanation.”
“You agree with it?”
“I said it was possible, not that it was probable. You do not consider it likely yourself?”
“I doubt Flora would hurt a fly.”
“Still, jealousy can transform a person remarkably. What is your own explanation of these events?”

“Really, I came here seeking an explanation, not offering one. I have told you all the facts. Since you ask, however, I have wondered whether the excitement, and the knowledge that she had risen so enormously in society, might have caused a slight nervous disturbance in my wife.”
“In other words, that she suddenly lost her reason?”
“Well, considering that she has turned her back—I will not say on me, but on advantages so many have sought in vain—I really can scarcely account for it otherwise.”

“Certainly another conceivable explanation,” Holmes said, smiling. “I think I now have almost all the information I need, Lord St. Simon. One question: from your place at the breakfast-table, could you see through the window?”
“We could see across the road to the Park.”
“Good. Then I do not think I need keep you here any longer. I shall contact you.”
“If you are fortunate enough to solve the mystery,” our client said, rising.
“It is already solved.”
“Eh? What did you say?”
“I said I have solved it.”
“Then where is my wife?”
“I shall soon provide that particular detail.”
Lord St. Simon shook his head. “I fear wiser men than either of us will be needed,” he said. With a formal, old-fashioned bow, he departed.

“How kind of his lordship to honour my intellect by placing it alongside his own,” Holmes said, laughing. “After all those questions, I think I shall take a whisky and soda and a cigar. I had reached my conclusions before he entered the room.”
“My dear Holmes!”

“I have records of several similar cases, though, as I said, none that developed so promptly. My questions merely changed conjecture into certainty. Circumstantial evidence can be very persuasive: finding a trout in the milk, for example, as Thoreau put it.”
“But I heard everything that you heard.”

“Without the knowledge of earlier cases that helps me so much. There was a parallel affair in Aberdeen some years ago, and a very similar one in Munich the year after the Franco-Prussian War. This belongs to that class—but here is Lestrade! Good afternoon! There is another glass on the sideboard, and cigars in the box.”
The police detective wore a pea-jacket and cravat, giving him a distinctly seafaring appearance. He carried a black canvas bag. After a brief greeting he sat down and lit the cigar Holmes offered.
“Well, what is the trouble?” Holmes asked, eyes twinkling. “You look unhappy.”
“I am unhappy. This damned St. Simon wedding case! I cannot make sense of any of it.”
“Really! That surprises me.”
“Who ever heard of such a muddle? Every clue slips out of my grasp. I have spent the whole day on it.”
“And the work seems to have made you very wet,” Holmes said, resting his hand on the pea-jacket’s sleeve.
“Yes. I have been dragging the Serpentine.”
“What on earth for?”
“I was searching for the body of Lady St. Simon.”
Sherlock Holmes reclined in his chair and laughed heartily.
“Have you also dragged the fountain basin in Trafalgar Square?” he asked.
“Why? What are you suggesting?”
“You have as much chance of finding this lady in one place as the other.”
Lestrade glared at him. “I suppose you know everything about it,” he growled.
“I have only just heard the facts, but I have reached a conclusion.”
“Indeed! Then you believe the Serpentine has nothing to do with it?”
“I consider that very improbable.”

“Perhaps you can explain why we found these in it.” He opened his bag and tipped a wedding dress of watered silk, white satin shoes, and a bridal wreath and veil onto the floor. All were stained and sodden. He set a new wedding ring on the heap. “There is a little puzzle for you, Master Holmes.”
“Indeed!” My friend blew blue smoke rings into the air. “You dragged these from the Serpentine?”
“No. A park-keeper found them floating near the bank. They have been identified as hers. I thought that where the clothes were, the body might not be far away.”
“By that splendid logic, every man must be found beside his wardrobe. And what exactly did you hope to establish by doing this?”
“Evidence connecting Flora Millar with the disappearance.”
“I fear you will have difficulty finding that.”

“Do you indeed!” Lestrade exclaimed bitterly. “Your deductions and inferences strike me as impractical, Holmes. You have made two mistakes in as many minutes. This dress does connect Miss Millar with the affair.”
“In what way?”

“The dress has a pocket; inside is a card-case; inside that is a note. Here it is.” He slapped it onto the table. “Listen: ‘You will see me when all is ready. Come at once. F. H. M.’ My theory has always been that Flora Millar enticed Lady St. Simon away and caused her disappearance, undoubtedly with accomplices. Here is the actual note, signed with her initials, which must have been secretly passed to the bride at the door, drawing her into their power.”

“Excellent, Lestrade,” Holmes said, laughing. “Quite remarkable. Let me look.” He took up the piece of paper in a casual, almost listless manner, but instantly became absorbed and gave a small exclamation of satisfaction. “This is important indeed.”
“Ah! You agree now?”
“Extremely important. My warm congratulations.”
Lestrade rose triumphantly and bent to look. “Why,” he cried, “you are reading the wrong side!”
“On the contrary, this is the right side.”
“The right side? You are mad! The pencil note is on this side.”
“And this side seems to contain part of a hotel bill, which interests me greatly.”

“Nothing in that. I have already examined it,” Lestrade replied. “‘October fourth: rooms, eight shillings; breakfast, two shillings and sixpence; cocktail, one shilling; lunch, two shillings and sixpence; glass of sherry, eightpence.’ I see nothing there.”
“Quite possibly. Nevertheless, it matters very much. The note itself matters too, or at least its initials do. Once again, my congratulations.”

“I have wasted enough time,” Lestrade said, getting up. “I believe in working, not sitting by a fire inventing theories. Good day, Mr. Holmes. We shall see who solves it first.” He bundled the clothes into his bag and headed for the door.
“Just one final hint for you, Lestrade,” Holmes drawled before he left. “I will give you the real answer. Lady St. Simon is a fiction. No such person exists, or ever has existed.”
Lestrade gave Holmes a sorrowful look. Turning to me, he tapped his forehead three times, solemnly shook his head, and hurried out.

Scarcely had the door shut when Holmes rose and put on his overcoat. “There is something in what he says about working outside,” he remarked. “I must leave you with your newspapers for a while, Watson.”

It was after five when Holmes went out, but I had little time to feel lonely. Within an hour, a confectioner’s delivery man arrived with an enormous flat box and a young assistant. They unpacked it, and to my astonishment began arranging a luxurious cold supper on our modest lodging-house table. Four cold woodcock, a pheasant, a _pâté de foie gras_ pie, and several ancient, cobwebbed bottles appeared. Once these delicacies were set out, the two men vanished like genii from the Arabian Nights. Their only explanation was that everything had been paid for and ordered to this address.
Shortly before nine, Sherlock Holmes entered the room briskly. His face was serious, but there was a brightness in his eyes that suggested events had not disappointed him in his conclusions.
“So supper is ready,” he said, rubbing his hands.
“You must be expecting guests. There are five places.”
“Yes, I think we may have visitors. I am surprised Lord St. Simon is not here already. Ah! I think that sounds like his step on the stairs.”
It was indeed our visitor from the afternoon who came hurrying into the room, swinging his glasses more vigorously than before. His aristocratic face looked deeply troubled.
“My messenger found you?” Holmes asked.
“Yes. I confess your message astonished me beyond measure. Have you good authority for everything you say?”
“As reliable as possible.”
Lord St. Simon dropped into a chair and rubbed his forehead.
“What will the Duke say,” he murmured, “when he learns that a member of his family has suffered such humiliation?”
“It was pure accident. I cannot agree that any humiliation is involved.”
“Ah, you view these matters from quite a different position.”
“I see no one to blame. The lady could scarcely have acted otherwise, though her abrupt way of doing so was regrettable. Without a mother, she had nobody to advise her at such a crisis.”
“It was an insult, sir. A public insult,” Lord St. Simon said, drumming his fingers on the table.
“You must allow for the extraordinary position in which the poor woman found herself.”
“I shall make no allowances. I am exceedingly angry and have been disgracefully treated.”

“I thought I heard the bell,” Holmes said. “Yes, footsteps on the landing. If I cannot persuade you to be generous, Lord St. Simon, I have found someone who may plead the case more successfully.” He opened the door and admitted a man and woman. “Allow me to introduce Mr. and Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton. You have met the lady, I believe.”

At their entrance, our client sprang up and stood stiffly erect, eyes lowered and one hand thrust deep inside the breast of his frock-coat: the very image of injured dignity. The woman quickly approached with an outstretched hand, but he would not look up. Perhaps it was just as well for his determination, for her appealing expression would have been difficult to resist.
“You are angry, Robert,” she said. “I guess you have every reason.”
“Please do not apologise to me,” he answered bitterly.

“Yes, I know I treated you terribly, and I should have spoken before leaving. But I was so rattled that from the moment I saw Frank again, I scarcely knew what I was doing or saying. I am only surprised I did not faint right there at the altar.”
“Mrs. Moulton, would you prefer my friend and me to leave the room while you explain the matter?”

“If I may say so,” the newcomer remarked, “there has already been too much secrecy. I would like all Europe and America to hear the truth.” He was small, wiry, and sunburnt, with a clean-shaven, sharp-featured face and alert movements.

“Then I will tell it now,” she said. “Frank and I met in 1884 at McQuire’s camp near the Rockies, where Pa was working a claim. We got engaged. Then one day Pa struck a rich pocket and made a fortune, while poor Frank’s claim dwindled away to nothing. As Pa grew richer, Frank grew poorer. Finally Pa refused to let the engagement continue and took me to San Francisco. Frank would not give up, though. He followed me there, and we met without Pa knowing anything about it. Knowing would only have enraged him, so we arranged everything ourselves. Frank promised to make his own fortune and not return to claim me until he was as wealthy as Pa. I promised to wait forever and never marry anyone else while he lived. ‘Why not marry now?’ he asked. ‘Then I can be sure of you, and I will not claim my place as your husband until I return.’ We discussed it, and he had arranged everything so well, with a clergyman waiting, that we married then and there. Frank went away to seek his fortune, and I returned to Pa.

“Next I heard, Frank was in Montana. Then he prospected in Arizona, and later I heard news of him from New Mexico. After that, a long newspaper report described an Apache attack on a miners’ camp. Frank’s name appeared among the dead. I fainted and remained ill for months. Pa thought I had a wasting illness and took me to half the doctors in San Francisco. For a year and more, not a single word of news arrived, and I never doubted Frank was dead. Then Lord St. Simon visited San Francisco, we came to London, and a marriage was arranged. Pa was delighted. But all along I knew nobody on earth could take poor Frank’s place in my heart.

“Still, had I married Lord St. Simon, I would have done my duty. We cannot control whom we love, but we can control our conduct. I went to the altar intending to be the best wife I could. Imagine my feelings, then, when I reached the altar rails, looked back, and saw Frank standing in the front pew, watching me. At first I thought him a ghost. But I looked again, and there he remained, his eyes seeming to ask whether I was glad or sorry to see him. Even now I am amazed that I did not collapse on the spot. Everything spun around me, and the clergyman’s words sounded like a bee buzzing in my ear. What should I do? Stop the service and cause a scene? I looked at Frank again. He seemed to understand, for he put a finger to his lips, asking me to keep quiet. Then he scribbled on a piece of paper, and I knew it was a message for me. Passing his pew on the way out, I dropped my bouquet to him. When he returned it, he slipped the note into my hand. It simply told me to join him when he signalled. I had no doubt that my first duty now belonged to him, and resolved to do whatever he directed.

“Back at the house, I told my maid. She had known Frank in California and had always been his friend. I instructed her to keep quiet, pack a few things, and prepare my ulster. I know I should have told Lord St. Simon, but speaking before his mother and all those grand people was terribly hard. I decided to escape first and explain later. Less than ten minutes after we sat down, I saw Frank across the road through the window. He beckoned and began walking into the Park. I slipped away, put on my things, and followed. A woman approached and said something about Lord St. Simon. From what little I heard, he seemed to have a premarital secret of his own. But I managed to get away and soon caught up with Frank. We took a cab to lodgings he had rented in Gordon Square. After all those years of waiting, that was my real wedding. Frank had been held captive by the Apaches. He escaped, returned to San Francisco, learned that I believed him dead and had gone to England, and followed me. He finally found me on the very morning of my second wedding.”
“I read it in a newspaper,” the American explained. “It named her and the church, but gave no home address.”

“We discussed what to do next. Frank wanted everything to be open and above board, but I felt so ashamed that I wanted to disappear and never face any of them again—perhaps only send a little note to Pa to say I was alive. It was dreadful even to think of all those lords and ladies sitting around the breakfast-table and waiting for me to return. Frank bundled up my wedding clothes and other things to prevent us being traced and dropped them somewhere he thought nobody would find them. We would probably have left for Paris tomorrow if this kind gentleman, Mr. Holmes, had not called this evening. How he found us I cannot imagine. He explained very kindly and clearly that Frank was right, I was wrong, and secrecy would put us in the wrong. Then he offered us the opportunity to speak privately with Lord St. Simon, so we came straight here. Now, Robert, you know everything. I am very sorry for any pain I have caused, and hope you do not think too badly of me.”
Throughout the whole of this lengthy account, Lord St. Simon remained rigid, his forehead furrowed and his lips pressed tightly together.
“Forgive me,” he said, “but I do not generally discuss my most private affairs in this public fashion.”
“Then you will not forgive me? Or shake hands before I leave?”
“Certainly, if that would give you any pleasure.” He held out his hand and coldly clasped the one she offered him.
“I had hoped you might share a friendly supper with us,” Holmes suggested.

“I think that is asking rather too much of me,” his lordship replied. “I may be obliged to accept these unexpected developments, but you can hardly expect me to celebrate them. With your permission, I shall wish you all good night.” He gave us a sweeping bow and strode out.

“Then I hope you two will honour me by staying,” Holmes said. “Meeting an American always gives me pleasure, Mr. Moulton. I believe that a king’s folly and a minister’s blunders in distant years will not prevent our children one day belonging to the same worldwide nation, beneath a flag combining the Union Jack and the Stars and Stripes in its quarters.”

“This has been an interesting case,” Holmes remarked after our guests had departed. “It shows very clearly how simple the explanation can be for something that at first appears almost inexplicable. Nothing could be more natural than the events she described, yet nothing could seem stranger than their result as viewed by, for instance, Mr. Lestrade of Scotland Yard.”
“Then you were never mistaken at any point?”

“From the very beginning, two facts were perfectly clear to me. She willingly took part in the wedding, yet regretted it within minutes of arriving home. Something that morning must have changed her mind. What? She could not have spoken privately with anyone while out: the bridegroom was beside her. Had she perhaps seen someone, then? If so, it must be someone from America. She had spent too little time here for anyone to gain such influence that merely seeing him could completely alter her plans. By excluding alternatives, we have already reached the possibility that she saw an American. Who could this American be, then, and why should he have so powerful an influence over her? A lover, perhaps, or a husband. I knew her early womanhood had been spent in rough surroundings under unusual conditions. That was the point I had already reached before I ever heard Lord St. Simon relate his account. His account supplied the man in the pew, her changed manner, the transparent device of dropping the bouquet to obtain a note, her consultation with a trusted maid, and the significant reference to jumping a claim. To miners, that means taking something to which another person already has a right. The entire situation became clear. She had left with a man, either her lover or an earlier husband, and the balance of probability favoured the latter explanation.”
“But how on earth did you locate them?”

“It might have been difficult. Fortunately Lestrade held information whose value he did not understand. The initials mattered greatly, of course. Still more useful was learning that the man had paid a bill at one of London’s most exclusive hotels within the past week.”
“How did you infer that it was exclusive?”

“From its exclusive prices. Eight shillings for a bed and eightpence for sherry suggested a very expensive establishment. Few London hotels charge so much. At the second one I visited in Northumberland Avenue, the register showed that an American, Francis H. Moulton, had left only yesterday. Examining his account, I found the precise entries from the duplicate bill. His letters were to follow him to 226 Gordon Square. I therefore went to that address and was fortunate enough to find the affectionate couple at home. I ventured to give the couple a little fatherly advice, explaining that everyone would benefit if they made their situation clearer to the public generally and Lord St. Simon particularly. I invited them to come here and meet him and, as you saw, ensured that he kept the appointment.”
“Without much success,” I observed. “His behaviour certainly could not be described as very gracious.”

“Ah, Watson,” Holmes replied with a smile, “perhaps you would not be gracious either if, after all the effort of courtship and marriage, you suddenly lost both wife and fortune. Let us judge Lord St. Simon generously and thank our stars we are unlikely ever to share his predicament. Pull up your chair and pass me the violin. Our only remaining problem is how to pass these bleak autumn evenings.”

chapters.title: The Beryl Coronet
paragraphs: “Holmes,” I said one morning from our bow-window, looking down the street, “a madman is approaching. It is rather sad that his family allows him to go out alone.”

My friend rose slowly from his armchair and looked over my shoulder, his hands in his dressing-gown pockets. The February morning was bright and crisp. Yesterday’s snow still lay deep, sparkling in the winter sun. Traffic had churned the centre of Baker Street into a crumbling brown strip, but at the sides and along the piled edges of the pavements it remained white. The grey paving had been cleared and scraped, yet was dangerously slippery, leaving fewer pedestrians than usual. Indeed, from the direction of the Metropolitan Station, nobody approached except the gentleman whose strange behaviour had caught my attention.

He was about fifty, tall, stout, and imposing, with a large, strongly marked face and a commanding presence. His sombre clothes were expensive: a black frock-coat, polished hat, neat brown gaiters, and well-tailored pearl-grey trousers. Yet his movements absurdly contradicted the dignity of both his clothing and his features. He ran hard, occasionally giving the little jumps of an exhausted man unaccustomed to exerting his legs. As he ran, his hands jerked up and down, his head shook, and his face twisted into extraordinary expressions.
“What on earth is wrong with him?” I asked. “He keeps looking at the house numbers.”
“I believe he is coming here,” Holmes replied, rubbing his hands.
“To us?”

“Yes. I suspect he wants professional advice. I believe I recognise the symptoms of such a visit. Ah! What did I tell you?” The man rushed to our door, panting, and pulled the bell until its clanging filled the house.

Moments later he stood in our room, still gasping and waving his arms. But the settled grief and despair in his eyes changed our smiles instantly into horror and pity. At first he could not speak. He swayed and tugged at his hair like someone pushed to the very limits of reason. Suddenly he sprang up and struck his head against the wall so violently that we rushed forward and dragged him to the middle of the room. Holmes pressed him into the armchair, sat beside him, and patted his hand, talking in the easy, reassuring tones he knew so well how to use.
“You came to tell me your story, did you not?” he said. “Your haste has exhausted you. Wait until you have recovered, and then I shall gladly examine whatever problem you wish to put before me.”
For a minute or more the man sat with his chest heaving, struggling against his emotions. Then he wiped his forehead, pressed his lips together, and turned towards us.
“You must think I am mad,” he said.
“I can see you have suffered some great trouble,” Holmes answered.

“God knows I have! Something so sudden and terrible it could drive me out of my mind. I might have endured public disgrace, though my reputation has never carried a stain. Private sorrow also comes to everyone. But both together, in such a dreadful form, have shaken me to the soul. Nor am I the only one concerned. The noblest people in the land may suffer unless we find a way out of this horrible situation.”
“Try to compose yourself, sir,” Holmes said. “Tell me clearly who you are and what has happened to you.”
“My name will probably already be familiar to you,” our visitor replied. “Alexander Holder, of Holder & Stevenson, the Threadneedle Street bankers.”

We certainly recognised the name of the senior partner in the City of London’s second-largest private bank. What could have reduced one of London’s leading citizens to such a pitiable state? We waited eagerly as he made another effort to collect himself and began his account.

“I feel that time is precious,” he said. “That is why I hurried here when the police inspector advised me to seek your help. I took the Underground to Baker Street and ran from the station, since cabs move slowly through this snow. I take very little exercise, which explains my breathlessness. I feel better now and shall give you the facts as briefly and clearly as possible.

“You know, of course, that successful banking depends just as much on finding profitable investments for our funds as on extending our business connections and increasing the number of depositors. One of our most profitable ways of investing money is to lend it against security of unquestionable value. We have conducted a great deal of such business in recent years. Many noble families have received substantial advances from us, secured against their pictures, their libraries, or their silver plate.

“Yesterday morning, while I sat in my bank office, a clerk brought in a visiting card. The name startled me. It belonged to none other than—well, perhaps even to you I should say only that it is known in every household throughout the world, one of the very highest and most exalted names in England. Overwhelmed by the honour, I tried to express my feelings when he entered. But he immediately began discussing business, like a man anxious to finish an unpleasant task quickly.
“‘Mr. Holder,’ he said, ‘I have been informed that you are accustomed to advancing money.’
“‘The firm does, provided the security is sound,’ I replied.

“‘It is absolutely essential that I obtain fifty thousand pounds immediately,’ he said. ‘Naturally I could borrow ten times that trifling sum from my friends, but I much prefer a business arrangement and to conduct it myself. You can readily understand why a man in my position should avoid placing himself under obligations.’
“‘For how long would you need the money?’ I asked.

“‘A substantial sum of money falls due to me next Monday. I shall certainly repay your advance then, with whatever interest you consider proper. It is essential, however, that you provide the money immediately.’

“‘I would gladly advance it from my own funds without further discussion,’ I replied, ‘but the strain would be rather greater than my private resources could bear. If I act for the firm, fairness to my partner requires me to observe every normal business precaution, even in a case such as yours.’
“‘I would much prefer that,’ he answered, lifting a square black morocco-leather case from beside his chair. ‘You have no doubt heard of the Beryl Coronet?’
“‘One of the empire’s most precious public possessions,’ I replied.

“‘Exactly.’ He opened the case. The magnificent jewel lay inside, embedded in soft, flesh-coloured velvet. ‘There are thirty-nine enormous beryls,’ he said. ‘The value of the chased goldwork is incalculable. Even the lowest valuation would make the coronet worth twice the loan I request. I am willing to leave it as security.’
“I took the precious case into my hands and looked uncertainly from it to my distinguished client.
“‘Do you question its value?’ he asked.
“‘Certainly not. I only question—’

“‘Whether I ought to leave it here. You need not worry. I would never consider it unless I were absolutely certain of reclaiming it in four days. It is purely a matter of formality. Is the security adequate?’
“‘More than adequate.’

“‘Mr. Holder, you understand how strongly this demonstrates my trust in you, based on everything I have heard. I count on your discretion and on your refraining from any gossip about the matter, but above all on your taking every possible precaution to protect the coronet. You will appreciate the enormous public scandal if it suffers any kind of harm. Damage would be almost as serious as losing it entirely: no other beryls in the world match these, and replacing them would be impossible. Nevertheless, I leave it with complete confidence and shall collect it myself on Monday morning.’

“Seeing how anxious my client was to leave, I said nothing further. I summoned my cashier and instructed him to hand over fifty thousand-pound notes. But once I was alone again, with the precious case on the table before me, I began to feel uneasy about the enormous responsibility I had assumed. Since the coronet belonged to the nation, any mishap would unquestionably cause a dreadful scandal. I already regretted having agreed to take charge of it. It was too late to change matters, however, so I locked it in my private safe and returned to my work.

“That evening I felt it would be unwise to leave such a treasure at the office. Bank safes had been broken into before; why not mine? If that happened, what a terrible position I should find myself in! I decided to carry the case back and forth for the next few days, so that it would never really pass beyond my reach. Accordingly I called a cab and drove to my Streatham house with the jewel. Only after taking it upstairs and locking it in my dressing-room bureau did I breathe freely.

“Let me describe my household, Mr. Holmes, so that you understand the situation completely. My groom and page sleep elsewhere and can be dismissed from consideration. Three maidservants have been with me for years and are entirely above suspicion. A fourth, the second waiting-maid, Lucy Parr, arrived only a few months ago. Her references were excellent, however, and her work has always satisfied me. She is very pretty and has attracted admirers who sometimes linger about the property. That is her only drawback. In every other respect we believe her to be a thoroughly good girl.

“That covers the servants. My family is small and quickly described. I am a widower with one son, Arthur. He has disappointed me deeply, Mr. Holmes. I am sure the fault is mine. People tell me that I have spoiled him, and very likely they are right. After my dear wife died, I felt he was all I had left to love. I could not bear his smile to fade even momentarily, and never denied him anything. Greater firmness might have served us both better, but I meant only to do what was best.

“Naturally it was my intention that he should eventually succeed me in the banking business. But he had no head for business. He was wild and wilful, and frankly I could not trust him with substantial sums. As a young man he joined an aristocratic club. His charming manners soon made him intimate with wealthy men of expensive tastes. He learned to gamble heavily at cards and squander money on racing. Again and again he begged for advances on his allowance to settle debts of honour. He made more than one attempt to break free of the dangerous company he was keeping, but his friend Sir George Burnwell always exerted enough influence to draw him back.

“Indeed, I can hardly be surprised that such a man as Sir George should gain this influence over my son. Arthur has frequently brought him to the house, and I too find his charm almost irresistible. He is older than Arthur, a thoroughly worldly man who seems to have been everywhere and seen everything, a brilliant conversationalist and strikingly handsome. Yet when I consider him calmly, away from the glamour of his presence, his cynical remarks and a look I have caught in his eyes convince me that he deserves profound distrust. My little Mary agrees with this judgement. She has a woman’s swift insight into character.

“Mary is the last person to describe. My niece, she was left alone when my brother died five years ago. I adopted her and have regarded her as my daughter ever since. She lights up our home: sweet, affectionate, beautiful, an excellent manager and housekeeper, yet as gentle, quiet, and tender as any woman could be. She is my right hand; I cannot imagine managing without her. Only in one matter has she opposed my wishes. Arthur loves her devotedly and has twice proposed marriage, but she refused him both times. If anyone could have guided him onto a better path, it was she. Marriage might have transformed his life. Now, alas, it is too late—too late forever!
“Now you know who lives in my house, Mr. Holmes. I shall continue this miserable account.

“Over coffee in the drawing-room after dinner, I told Arthur and Mary about the day’s events and the treasure under our roof, withholding only my client’s identity. I am certain Lucy Parr, who served the coffee, had left the room, though I cannot swear the door was shut. Arthur and Mary were fascinated and wanted to see the famous coronet. I thought it better to leave it undisturbed.
“‘Where did you put it?’ Arthur asked.
“‘In my own bureau upstairs.’
“‘Well, I hope to goodness burglars don’t visit us tonight,’ he said.
“‘It is locked away,’ I answered.
“‘Any old key opens that bureau. As a boy I unlocked it myself using the key to the box-room cupboard.’
“He often spoke wildly, so I gave what he said very little thought. Later that night, however, he followed me upstairs looking very serious.
“‘Listen, Father,’ he said, eyes lowered. ‘Could you give me two hundred pounds?’
“‘No!’ I replied sharply. ‘I have been far too generous over money already.’
“‘You have been very kind,’ he admitted. ‘But without this money I can never show my face at the club again.’
“‘And a very good thing!’ I exclaimed.
“‘You would not want me to leave in disgrace,’ he said. ‘I could not bear that. Somehow I must find the money. If you will not give it to me, I shall have to try elsewhere.’
“I was furious: this was his third demand that month. ‘Not one farthing will you get from me!’ I cried. He bowed and left without another word.

“After he left, I opened the bureau, checked that the treasure was safe, and locked it again. Then I went round the house to check its security. Usually Mary does this, but that night I wanted to see to it myself. Coming downstairs, I found her at the hall’s side window. She closed and fastened it as I approached.
“‘Father,’ she said, looking slightly troubled, I thought, ‘did you give Lucy permission to go out tonight?’
“‘Certainly I did not.’
“‘She has just come in through the back door. I have no doubt she only went to the side gate to meet someone, but I think it unsafe and feel it should stop.’
“‘Speak to her tomorrow morning, or I will if you prefer. Are you quite sure that everything is securely fastened?’
“‘Quite certain, Father.’
“‘Then good night.’ I kissed her, returned to my bedroom, and soon fell asleep.
“I am trying to tell you everything that might have any bearing on the case, Mr. Holmes. Please question me about any point that I have not made entirely clear.”
“On the contrary, your account is unusually clear.”

“The next part is one I particularly want to describe precisely. I am not normally a heavy sleeper, and my anxiety probably made me sleep even more lightly than usual. At about two in the morning, some noise inside the house woke me. It stopped before I was fully awake, but left the impression that somewhere a window had been gently shut. I lay listening as hard as I could. Suddenly, to my horror, I distinctly heard footsteps moving softly in the adjoining room. My heart pounding with fear, I slipped out of bed and peered around the corner of my dressing-room door.
“‘Arthur!’ I screamed. ‘You villain! You thief! How dare you lay hands on that coronet?’

“The gas still burned half high, as I had left it. My unhappy son stood beside the light in only his shirt and trousers, the coronet in his hands. He seemed to be twisting or bending it with all his strength. At my cry he dropped it and went deathly pale. I seized and examined it. One gold corner containing three beryls was gone.
“‘You scoundrel!’ I shouted, wild with anger. ‘You have ruined it! Disgraced me forever! Where are the jewels you stole?’
“‘Stole!’ he exclaimed.
“‘Yes, thief!’ I shouted, shaking his shoulder.
“‘Nothing is missing. Nothing can be missing,’ he replied.
“‘Three stones are missing, and you know where they are. Must I call you a liar as well as a thief? Did I not see you trying to break off another piece?’
“‘You have insulted me enough,’ he said. ‘I will endure no more. Since you choose to abuse me, I shall say nothing further about this affair. Tomorrow morning I leave your house and make my own way.’
“‘You will leave in police custody!’ I cried, half mad with grief and rage. ‘I shall have this investigated to the very bottom.’
“‘You will learn nothing from me,’ he said with a passion I had never thought him capable of. ‘Call the police if you wish. Let them discover whatever they can.’

“My angry shouting had now woken everyone. Mary rushed in first. One look at the coronet and Arthur’s face told her the whole story; she screamed and fainted. I sent the housemaid for the police and immediately put the enquiry in their hands. Arthur had remained standing there sullenly with his arms folded across his chest. When an inspector and constable arrived, he asked whether I intended to charge him with theft. I told him it was no longer a private affair: the damaged coronet belonged to the nation. I was determined to let the law take its course in every respect.
“‘At least do not arrest me immediately,’ he said. ‘Allow me to go outside for five minutes. It would serve your interests as well as mine.’

“‘To escape, or perhaps hide what you have stolen,’ I replied. Then, fully realising my dreadful position, I implored him to remember once more that not only my honour but that of someone far greater was at stake. He threatened a scandal that would shake the nation. He could prevent it all simply by saying what he had done with the three missing stones.

“‘Face the facts,’ I urged. ‘You were caught in the act. Confessing cannot make your guilt worse. Do what you can to repair the damage: tell us where the beryls are, and everything will be forgiven and forgotten.’

“‘Save your forgiveness for those who want it,’ he answered, turning away with a sneer. He was too hardened for anything I said to move him. Only one course remained. I called the inspector and gave my son into custody. They immediately searched him, his bedroom, and every part of the house where he could possibly have hidden the stones. Nothing was found. Neither persuasion nor threats could make the wretched boy speak. This morning they took him to a cell. After completing the police formalities, I hurried here to beg you to use your abilities to solve the matter. The police freely admit that at present it defeats them. Spend whatever you think necessary. I have already offered a thousand-pound reward. My God, what am I to do! In one night I have lost my honour, my jewels, and my son. Oh, what can I do!”
He pressed his hands against the sides of his head and rocked back and forth, making a low, wordless sound like a child whose grief has passed beyond speech.
Sherlock Holmes sat without speaking for several minutes, frowning and staring intently into the fire.
“Do you have many visitors?” he asked.
“Only my partner and his family, and an occasional friend of Arthur’s. Sir George Burnwell has called several times recently. Nobody else, I think.”
“Do you attend many social engagements?”
“Arthur does. Mary and I prefer staying home. Neither of us enjoys society.”
“That is rather unusual in a young woman.”
“She is quiet by nature. Besides, she is not particularly young: twenty-four.”
“From your account, this has been a great shock to her as well.”
“Terrible! She is even more distressed than I am.”
“Neither you nor she has any doubt about your son’s guilt?”
“How could we, when I saw the coronet in his hands with my own eyes?”
“That scarcely seems conclusive. Was the remaining part of the coronet damaged?”
“Yes. It was bent out of shape.”
“Do you not think he might have been trying to straighten it, then?”
“God bless you! You are doing your best for us both. But it is hopeless. Why was he there at all? If he meant no harm, why did he not say so?”
“Exactly. And if he meant harm, why not invent a lie? His silence seems capable of either interpretation. Several aspects are unusual. What did the police make of the sound that woke you?”
“They thought it might have been Arthur closing his bedroom door.”
“A fine explanation! As though a man planning a crime would slam his door and wake the household. What do they say about the missing jewels?”
“They are still tapping the floorboards and examining the furniture, hoping to locate them.”
“Have they thought of searching outside the house?”
“Yes. They have been remarkably energetic. The whole garden has already been thoroughly searched.”

“Surely you see, my dear sir,” Holmes said, “that the affair goes much deeper than either you or the police first supposed. You thought it simple; I find it exceedingly complicated. Consider everything involved in the explanation you have put forward. Your son gets out of bed, risks entering your dressing-room, unlocks the bureau, removes the coronet, and forcibly breaks off a piece. He goes elsewhere and hides three of its thirty-nine jewels so skilfully that nobody can find them. Then he brings the remaining thirty-six back into the very room where he runs the greatest risk of discovery. Now I ask you, is such a theory really credible?”
“What other explanation is there?” the banker cried despairingly. “If his intentions were innocent, why does he not tell us?”
“We must discover that,” Holmes replied. “Now, Mr. Holder, let us go together to Streatham and devote an hour to looking a little more closely at all these details.”

My friend insisted that I should accompany them on their expedition, which I was eager enough to do. The story had deeply stirred both my curiosity and sympathy. I admit Arthur’s guilt seemed as clear to me as to his unhappy father. Yet my faith in Holmes’s judgement was such that, while he questioned the accepted explanation, I felt there must be hope. Throughout the journey to the southern suburb he scarcely spoke, sitting with his chin lowered to his chest and his hat over his eyes, absorbed in thought. Our client seemed encouraged by the faint possibility we had offered. He even began a wandering conversation with me about his business. A short train journey and a still shorter walk brought us to Fairbank, the great financier’s modest home.

Fairbank was a substantial square house of white stone set a little back from the road. Two branches of a carriage drive, enclosing a snow-covered lawn, led to large iron entrance gates. On the right a small wooden thicket led to a narrow path between tidy hedges, running from the road to the kitchen door: the tradesmen’s entrance. To the left, outside the property, a public but little-used lane led to the stables. Leaving us at the door, Holmes slowly circled the house, crossed the front, followed the tradesmen’s path, and went around the rear garden into the stable lane. He was gone so long that Mr. Holder and I went into the dining-room and waited beside the fire for his return. We sat silently until a young woman entered. Slightly taller than average and slender, she had dark hair and eyes made darker still by her extraordinary pallor. I have never seen a woman’s face so deathly white. Her lips too lacked colour, while her eyes were red from crying. She moved silently into the room, giving an even stronger impression of grief than the banker that morning. It was striking because she clearly had great strength of character and self-control. Ignoring me, she went directly to her uncle and tenderly stroked his head.
“You have given orders for Arthur to be released, haven’t you, Father?” she asked.
“No, my dear. We must get to the bottom of this.”
“But I am certain he is innocent. You know a woman’s instincts. I know he has done nothing wrong, and you will regret treating him so harshly.”
“Why will he not speak, if he is innocent?”
“Who can say? Perhaps your suspicion made him too angry.”
“How could I avoid suspecting him when I actually saw him holding the coronet?”
“He had only picked it up to examine it. Please, please believe me: he is innocent. Drop the matter and say no more. The thought of our dear Arthur in prison is unbearable!”

“Never until the jewels are found, Mary! Your love for Arthur blinds you to the dreadful consequences for me. Instead of suppressing the affair, I have brought a gentleman from London to investigate it further.”
“This gentleman?” she asked, turning towards me.
“No, his friend. He wanted to work alone. He is in the stable lane now.”
“The stable lane?” Her dark eyebrows rose. “What could he find there? Ah, that must be him. Sir, I hope you will prove what I am certain is true: my cousin Arthur did not commit this crime.”
“I entirely agree, and share your hope that we can prove it,” Holmes replied, returning to the mat to stamp snow from his shoes. “I believe you are Miss Mary Holder. May I ask one or two questions?”
“Certainly, sir, if it will help resolve this dreadful affair.”
“You heard nothing yourself last night?”
“Nothing until my uncle raised his voice. I heard him then and came downstairs.”
“You secured the house last night. Did you make certain that every window was fastened?”
“Yes.”
“Were all of them still fastened this morning?”
“Yes.”
“One maid has a sweetheart. You told your uncle last night that she had been out to see him, I believe?”
“Yes. She also served in the drawing-room and might have overheard my uncle speaking about the coronet.”
“I see. You suspect that she went outside to tell her sweetheart, and they may have arranged the theft together.”
“What use are these vague and uncertain suggestions,” the banker exclaimed impatiently, “when I have told you I saw Arthur holding the coronet?”
“Patience, Mr. Holder. We shall return to that. Miss Holder, you saw this maid come back through the kitchen door?”
“Yes. I was checking that it was locked for the night when she slipped in. I also saw the man in the darkness.”
“Do you recognise him?”
“Certainly! His name is Francis Prosper, and he is the greengrocer who delivers our vegetables.”
“He stood to the left of the door,” Holmes said, “farther along the path than someone approaching the door would need to go?”
“Yes, that is where he stood.”
“And he is a man with a wooden leg?”
Something like fear entered the young woman’s expressive dark eyes. “You are like a magician,” she said. “How could you know?” She smiled, but Holmes’s thin, intent face did not respond.
“I should like to go upstairs now,” he said. “I shall probably want to examine the grounds once more. Perhaps I had better inspect the lower windows before going up.”

He moved rapidly from window to window, pausing only at the large hall window overlooking the stable lane. He opened it and scrutinised the sill through his powerful lens. “Now we can go upstairs,” he said at last.
The banker’s dressing-room was small and simply furnished, with a grey carpet, a large bureau, and a tall mirror. Holmes went straight to the bureau and closely inspected its lock.
“Which key was used to open this?” he asked.
“The one my son mentioned: the lumber-room cupboard key.”
“Do you have it here?”
“There it is on the dressing-table.”
Holmes picked up the key and unlocked the bureau.

“The lock makes no sound,” he observed. “No wonder it failed to wake you. I assume this case holds the coronet. We must examine it.” He opened the case, lifted out the diadem, and placed it on the table. It was magnificent workmanship. Its thirty-six stones were the finest I had ever seen. One edge was fractured where a corner containing three jewels had been torn away.
“Now, Mr. Holder, this corner corresponds to the one so unfortunately lost. Would you be good enough to try to break it off?”
The banker drew back in horror. “I would never dream of attempting it.”

“Then I will.” Holmes suddenly applied all his strength, without success. “It yields slightly,” he said. “But despite my unusually strong fingers, breaking it would tax me to the utmost. An ordinary man could not manage it. And what would happen if I did succeed? It would make a noise like a pistol shot. Are you telling me that happened within yards of your bed and you heard nothing?”
“I cannot think what to believe. Everything is dark to me.”
“Perhaps it will become clearer as we proceed. What do you think, Miss Holder?”
“I admit I am as puzzled as my uncle.”
“Your son wore neither shoes nor slippers when you saw him?”
“He had on only his shirt and trousers. Nothing else.”

“Thank you. We have been extraordinarily fortunate in this enquiry. If we fail to explain it, we shall have only ourselves to blame. With your permission, Mr. Holder, I shall now resume my examination outside.”

At his request he went alone: unnecessary footprints, he explained, might complicate his task. He worked for an hour or more, finally returning with snow weighing down his shoes and his expression as unreadable as ever.
“I believe I have now seen everything there is to see, Mr. Holder. I can best help you by returning to my rooms.”
“But the jewels! Where are they, Mr. Holmes?”
“I cannot say.”
The banker wrung his hands. “I shall never recover them! And my son? Can you offer any hope?”
“My opinion remains exactly as before.”
“Then, for God’s sake, what dreadful events took place in my house last night?”

“Come to Baker Street between nine and ten tomorrow morning, and I shall gladly do everything I can to make the matter clearer. I understand you give me _carte blanche_, provided I recover the stones, and impose no limit on the money I may spend on your behalf.”
“I would surrender my fortune to recover them.”
“Very good. I shall work on it in the meantime. Goodbye. It is just possible that I may need to return here before evening.”

Plainly Holmes had settled the case in his own mind, though I could not begin to imagine his conclusions. On the way home I repeatedly tried to discover them. Each time he gently moved to another subject, until I gave up. It was not yet three when we reached our rooms in Baker Street. He hurried upstairs and soon reappeared dressed as an ordinary loafer: a shabby, shiny coat with its collar up, a red cravat, and worn boots. He looked the perfect example of an ordinary man belonging to that class.

“This should serve,” he said, inspecting himself in the mantelpiece mirror. “I wish you could come, Watson, but I fear it would not do. Perhaps I am on the right trail; perhaps chasing a will-o’-the-wisp. I shall soon find out. I hope that I shall be able to return within a few hours.” He sliced beef from the joint on the sideboard, put it between two rounds of bread, and pocketed this rough meal before setting off.
I had just finished tea when he returned in excellent spirits, swinging an old elastic-sided boot. He tossed it into a corner and poured himself a cup.
“Just stopping in on my way,” he said. “I must go straight on.”
“Where are you going?”
“Oh, to the other side of the West End. It may be quite some time before I return. Do not wait up if I am late.”
“How is the investigation progressing?”

“Well enough. I have nothing to complain about. I have been back to Streatham since we parted, though not to the house. A delightful little problem; I would not have missed it for a great deal. But I must stop gossiping, remove these disreputable clothes, and become my highly respectable self again.”

His manner showed that he had stronger reasons for satisfaction than his words suggested. His eyes sparkled, and even his sallow cheeks had gained a little colour. He hurried upstairs. A few minutes later the front door slammed, telling me that he had gone out again on the hunt he found so congenial.

I waited until midnight, then went to bed when he still had not returned. When he was following a promising trail, he often stayed away for days and nights at a time, so his late absence did not surprise me. I do not know when he came home. At breakfast, however, he was already downstairs, neat and fresh, holding coffee in one hand and a newspaper in the other.
“You will forgive me for starting without you, Watson,” he said. “Remember, our client has an early appointment today.”
“It is past nine already,” I replied. “That may be him now. I thought I heard the bell.”

Our visitor was indeed the financier, and the change in him shocked me. His face, naturally broad and massive, now looked pinched and hollow. Even his hair seemed to me at least a shade whiter. He entered with a weariness and lethargy more painful to witness than yesterday morning’s agitation, and sank heavily into the armchair I pushed forward for him.

“I do not know what I have done to deserve such trials,” he said. “Only two days ago I was a happy, prosperous man with no cares at all. Now my old age promises loneliness and disgrace. One sorrow follows another. My niece Mary has abandoned me.”
“Abandoned you?”

“Yes. Her bed had not been slept in this morning, her room was empty, and this note waited on the hall table. Last night I told her, sorrowfully rather than angrily, that everything might have gone well for Arthur if she had married him. Perhaps I spoke thoughtlessly. That is the remark she means here:

“‘Dearest Uncle,—I feel I have caused your troubles. Had I acted differently, this terrible misfortune might never have happened. Knowing that, I can never again be happy in your home, and must leave you forever. Do not worry about my future; it is provided for. Above all, do not try to find me. The search would be useless and would only harm me. In life or death, I remain your loving,
“‘MARY.’
“What does she mean, Mr. Holmes? Does this suggest she intends suicide?”
“No, certainly nothing of that kind. Perhaps this is the best outcome possible. I hope your troubles are nearly over, Mr. Holder.”
“Ah! You say that! You have heard something, learned something! Where are the jewels, Mr. Holmes?”
“Would a thousand pounds for each seem excessive to you?”
“I would give ten thousand.”
“Unnecessary. Three thousand will suffice. I believe there is also a reward. Do you have your cheque-book? Here is a pen. Make the cheque four thousand pounds.”
Looking bewildered, the banker wrote the cheque. Holmes crossed to his desk, took out a small triangular piece of gold containing three stones, and tossed it onto the table.
Our client seized it with a cry of delight.
“You found it!” he gasped. “I am saved! Saved!”
His joy was as overwhelming as his grief had been. He clasped the recovered jewels to his chest.
“There is something else that you still owe, Mr. Holder,” Holmes said rather sternly.
“Owe?” He grabbed a pen. “Tell me the amount and I will pay.”
“The debt is not to me. You owe your son a deeply humble apology. That noble young man has behaved as I should be proud to see a son of my own behave, if I ever have one.”
“Then Arthur did not take the stones?”
“I told you yesterday he did not. I repeat it today.”
“You are certain! Then let us hurry to him at once and tell him the truth has been discovered.”

“He already knows. Once I had cleared up the whole affair, I went and had an interview with him. When he refused to give me his account, I gave him mine. He had to admit I was right and supply the few details still unclear. Your news this morning, however, may make him speak.”
“For Heaven’s sake, explain this extraordinary mystery to me!”

“I will, including the steps that led me to the truth. First, though, comes what is hardest for me to say and for you to hear. Your niece Mary and Sir George Burnwell had a secret understanding. They have now run away together.”
“My Mary? That cannot be!”

“Unfortunately, it is not merely possible but certain. Neither you nor Arthur understood the man you admitted into your family. He is among England’s most dangerous men: a ruined gambler, utterly desperate, without heart or conscience. Your niece knew nothing of men like him. When he whispered promises, as he had to a hundred women before, she believed she alone had won his heart. The devil knows what he said. At any rate, she became his instrument and met him almost every evening.”
“I cannot and will not believe it!” the banker cried, his face ashen.

“Then let me describe the events in your house last night. Believing you had gone upstairs, Mary slipped down to speak with her lover through the window facing the stable lane. He stood there so long that his footprints pressed through the snow. She told him about the coronet. The news aroused his wicked greed, and he imposed his will on her. I am certain she loved you, but in some women love for a lover extinguishes every other affection. I think she must be one of them. Barely had she heard his instructions when she saw you descending. She quickly shut the window and mentioned the maid’s outing with her wooden-legged sweetheart. That story was entirely true.

“After speaking with you, Arthur went to bed, but worry over his club debts made him sleep badly. In the middle of the night, light footsteps passed his door. He got out of bed and looked into the passage, astonished to see his cousin creeping down the passage and into your dressing-room. Amazed, he put on some clothes and waited in the dark to see what would happen. Presently she emerged. By the light of the lamp in the passage he could see the precious coronet in her hands. She went downstairs. Horrified, he hurried along and hid behind the curtain near your door, where he could watch the hall below. He saw her quietly open the window and pass the coronet to someone outside. She shut it and hurried back to her room, passing close to his hiding place.

“As long as she remained on the scene, he could take no action without exposing the woman he loved. As soon as she left, however, he understood how disastrous this would be for you and how urgently it must be remedied. Barefoot as he was, he rushed downstairs, opened the window, jumped into the snow, and followed a dark figure down the moonlit lane. Sir George tried to escape, but Arthur caught him. They struggled, your son pulling on one side of the coronet and his opponent on the other. During the fight your son struck Sir George, cutting him above the eye. Something suddenly snapped. Finding himself holding the coronet, Arthur ran back, shut the window, and returned to your room. He had just noticed that the struggle had bent the coronet and was trying to straighten it when you appeared.”
“Can that be possible?” the banker gasped.

“Your accusations then enraged him, coming at the very moment when he felt he deserved your warmest gratitude. He could not explain the truth without betraying someone who deserved little consideration from him. Yet he chose the more chivalrous course and protected her secret.”

“That explains her scream and faint when she saw the coronet!” Mr. Holder exclaimed. “My God, what a blind fool I have been! And his request for five minutes outside! The dear boy wanted to search for the missing piece where they had fought. How cruelly I misjudged him!”

“On arriving,” Holmes continued, “I immediately examined the grounds carefully for useful marks in the snow. I knew no fresh snow had fallen since the evening before, and a hard frost had preserved the impressions. I walked along the tradesmen’s path, but the snow there had been trampled so thoroughly that separate footprints could not be distinguished. Just beyond it, past the kitchen door, a woman had talked with a man. Round marks on one side of his tracks revealed a wooden leg. I could even see that they had been interrupted. Deep toe marks and light heel marks showed the woman had run back to the door. The man with the wooden leg waited briefly, then departed. At the time I suspected these were the maid and her sweetheart, of whom you had already told me; subsequent questions confirmed that they were. In the garden I saw only scattered tracks, which I took to be the police’s. But the stable lane presented a long, intricate story written in snow.

“There were tracks of a booted man going both ways, and, to my delight, a second set made by bare feet. From your account I immediately identified the latter as Arthur’s. The first man had walked in both directions along the lane; the barefoot man had run. Here and there his prints overlaid the boot marks, clearly showing he came later. I followed the tracks carefully towards the house and reached the hall window, where the booted man had worn away all the snow while waiting. In the other direction, a hundred yards or more down the lane, I found the spot where the man in boots had turned round to face his pursuer. The snow was churned by a struggle. Drops of blood confirmed my reading. Afterwards the booted man ran farther down the lane; another small bloodstain showed he was the injured one. At the main road the pavement had been cleared, ending that trail.

“Inside, as you recall, I examined the hall window’s sill and frame with my lens. Someone had plainly climbed out. I also distinguished the outline of an instep left by a wet foot coming back in. The events now began to take shape. A man waited outside; someone brought him the jewels. Your son witnessed it, pursued the thief, and fought him. Each pulled on the coronet, their combined strength causing damage neither could have produced alone. Arthur returned with the prize, leaving a fragment in his opponent’s hands. Up to that point everything was quite clear to me. There were now just two questions remaining: who was the man, and who had brought him the coronet?

“One of my own longstanding principles is that once the impossible is excluded, whatever remains must be true, however unlikely. You had not brought it downstairs, so only your niece and the maids remained. But why would your son accept blame for a maid? There was no conceivable reason. His love for his cousin, however, provided an excellent reason to keep her secret, especially such a disgraceful secret.
