Remembering that you had seen her at the window, and that she fainted when the coronet reappeared, turned my suspicion into certainty.

“Who could have been her accomplice? Clearly a lover: who else could outweigh the love and gratitude she must feel towards you? I knew you seldom went into society and that your circle of friends was very small. Among them, however, was Sir George Burnwell. I already knew of his bad reputation with women. He must have worn those boots and kept the missing jewels. Even though he knew Arthur had recognised him, he could still imagine himself safe. The young man could not say a word without compromising his own family.

“You can guess my next steps. Disguised as a loafer, I visited Sir George’s house, befriended his valet, and learned that his master had cut his head the night before. For six shillings I bought a pair of his discarded shoes to settle the matter. With those shoes I travelled down to Streatham and found they matched the tracks exactly.”
“I saw a poorly dressed vagabond in that lane yesterday evening,” Mr. Holder said.

“Exactly. That was me. Now that I knew for certain I had found the right man, I went home to change. The next part that I had to play required considerable delicacy. To prevent scandal, prosecution had to be avoided, and a villain as clever as he was would recognise that our hands were tied. I went to his house and called on him. Naturally he denied everything at first. When I described every detail, however, he blustered and took a weighted club from the wall. I knew whom I was dealing with and pressed a pistol to his head before he could strike. That made him more reasonable. I offered a thousand pounds for each stone. That produced the very first signs of distress that he had shown. ‘Damn it!’ he exclaimed. ‘I sold all three for six hundred!’ Promising there would be no prosecution, I soon obtained the receiver’s address. After considerable bargaining with that man, I bought the stones for a thousand pounds each. Then I visited Arthur, told him everything was settled, and finally reached bed around two after a genuinely hard day’s work.”

“A day that spared England a great public scandal,” the banker said, rising. “Words cannot express my gratitude, sir, but you will not find me ungrateful. Your skill surpasses everything I have heard. Now I must hurry to my dear son and apologise for the wrong I have done him. What you tell me about poor Mary cuts me to the heart. Even you cannot tell me where she is now.”

“I think we can safely assume,” Holmes replied, “that she is wherever Sir George Burnwell may be. Equally certain is that, whatever wrong she has done, her punishment will soon be more than sufficient.”

chapters.title: The Copper Beeches
paragraphs: “For a man who loves art for its own sake,” Sherlock Holmes remarked, throwing aside the advertising pages of _The Daily Telegraph_, “the greatest pleasure often lies in its humblest and least important expressions. I am pleased to see, Watson, that you have understood this truth so far. In the little accounts of our cases that you have kindly written—and, I must admit, sometimes embellished—you give prominence less to the many _causes célèbres_ and sensational trials in which I have appeared than to incidents perhaps insignificant in themselves, but offering scope for those powers of deduction and logical synthesis which I have made my particular field.”
“Yet,” I replied, smiling, “I cannot consider myself entirely innocent of the sensationalism people accuse my accounts of displaying.”

“Your mistake, perhaps,” he observed, taking a glowing cinder in the tongs and using it to light his long cherrywood pipe—the one that usually replaced his clay pipe when he felt argumentative rather than reflective—“your mistake, perhaps, is trying to give colour and life to every statement instead of simply recording the rigorous reasoning from cause to effect which is really the only remarkable feature of the whole business.”

“It seems to me that I have done you full justice in this matter,” I replied rather coldly. I disliked the egotism that I had more than once noticed as a powerful element in my friend’s unusual character.

“It is neither vanity nor selfishness,” he answered, responding as usual to my thoughts rather than my words. “I ask justice for my art because it is impersonal, something beyond myself. Crime is ordinary; logic is rare. Concentrate on the logic, then, rather than the crime. You have reduced what should have been a series of lectures to a collection of stories.”

It was a cold early-spring morning. Breakfast over, we sat on either side of a cheerful fire in our familiar Baker Street room. Thick fog rolled between the dull brown houses, reducing the opposite windows to vague dark shapes behind heavy yellow clouds. The gaslight shone on the white tablecloth and gleaming china and metal, for breakfast had not yet been cleared. Holmes had been silent all morning, repeatedly searching the advertisements in one newspaper after another. Apparently abandoning the search, he finally emerged in a sour mood to lecture me on my literary failings.

After a pause, during which he sat puffing his long pipe and gazing down into the fire, he continued: “At the same time, you can scarcely be accused of sensationalism. A fair proportion of these cases in which you have kindly taken an interest involve no crime at all in the legal sense. The small matter in which I tried to help the King of Bohemia, Miss Mary Sutherland’s strange experience, the problem of the man with the twisted lip and the incident of the noble bachelor all lay outside the law’s concern. But in avoiding sensation, I fear you may have come close to triviality.”
“The outcome may have been trivial,” I replied. “The methods, I believe, were original and interesting.”

“My dear fellow, what does the public—the vast, unobservant public, scarcely able to recognise a weaver by his tooth or a compositor by his left thumb—care for fine distinctions in analysis and deduction? Yet I cannot blame your triviality. The great cases are over. Mankind, or at least criminal mankind, has lost all initiative and originality. My own practice is becoming an agency for finding lost pencils and advising schoolgirls. I think I have finally reached the bottom, however, with this letter that arrived this morning. I think it establishes my absolute zero. Read it!” He tossed me a crumpled sheet.
It was dated at Montague Place on the previous evening, and read as follows:

“Dear Mr. Holmes,—I urgently wish to ask your advice about whether to accept a position offered to me as a governess. Unless it inconveniences you, I shall call tomorrow at half-past ten. Yours faithfully,
“VIOLET HUNTER.”
“Do you know her?” I asked.
“Not at all.”
“It is half-past ten already.”
“Yes, and that is surely her at the bell.”
“It may be more interesting than you expect. Remember the blue carbuncle: at first it seemed a mere whim, yet it became a serious investigation. This case might develop in the same way.”
“Well, let us hope that is so. Our doubts will soon be resolved, for unless I am much mistaken, here comes the lady herself.”

The door opened as he spoke, admitting a young woman dressed simply but neatly. Her lively, intelligent face was freckled like a plover’s egg, and she had the brisk manner of someone who had made her own way in life.

“You will forgive me for troubling you, I am sure,” she said as my companion rose to greet her. “I have had a very strange experience. As I have neither parents nor relatives of any kind to advise me, I thought you might be kind enough to tell me what I ought to do.”
“Please sit down, Miss Hunter. I shall gladly do whatever I can to help you.”

I could see that the new client’s manner and speech had made a favourable impression on Holmes. He studied her with his searching gaze, then settled himself to listen to her account, eyelids lowered and fingertips pressed together.

“I have spent five years as a governess in Colonel Spence Munro’s family,” she said. “But two months ago the colonel received an appointment in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and took his children to America with him, leaving me without a position. I placed advertisements and answered others, but nothing came of either. Finally my small savings began to run low, and I was at my wits’ end, wondering what to do.

“In the West End there is a well-known agency for governesses called Westaway’s. I used to call there about once a week to ask whether any position suitable for me had become available. Westaway was the founder’s name, but Miss Stoper actually manages the business. She sits in her own small office while the women seeking work wait in an anteroom. They are shown in one at a time, and she consults her ledgers to see whether she has anything that would suit them.

“Last week I was shown into the office as usual, but Miss Stoper had company. An enormously stout man sat beside her, wearing glasses and closely examining each woman who entered. His face was all smiles; a great heavy chin folded down over his throat in successive rolls. At the sight of me he almost jumped in his chair and quickly turned to Miss Stoper.

“‘That is the one!’ he said. ‘I could ask for nothing better. Excellent! Excellent!’ He seemed delighted, rubbing his hands with great good humour. He looked so comfortable and pleasant that merely seeing him was a pleasure.
“‘Are you seeking employment, miss?’ he asked.
“‘Yes, sir.’
“‘As a governess?’
“‘Yes, sir.’
“‘What salary do you require?’
“‘Colonel Spence Munro paid me four pounds a month in my last position.’
“‘Tut, tut! Exploitation—sheer exploitation!’ He flung his fat hands into the air as though furious. ‘How could anyone offer such a miserable sum to a lady of your attractions and accomplishments?’
“‘You may overestimate my accomplishments, sir,’ I replied. ‘A little French and German, music, drawing—’

“‘Tut, tut! None of that is the point. Do you possess the manners and bearing of a lady? That is the whole question. If not, you cannot educate a child who may one day play an important part in this country’s history. But if you do, how could any gentleman ask you to accept less than three figures? Your starting salary with me, madam, would be a hundred pounds a year.’

“You can imagine, Mr. Holmes, that to someone as penniless as I was, this offer seemed almost too good to be true. Perhaps noticing the disbelief on my face, the gentleman opened his pocketbook and took out a banknote.

“‘It is also my usual practice,’ he said, smiling so pleasantly that his eyes became two small shining slits among the pale folds of his face, ‘to pay my young ladies half their salary in advance, so that they can meet any small expenses for their journey and their clothing.’

“I felt I had never met anyone so charming and considerate. Since I already owed money to my tradespeople, the advance would be a great convenience. Yet something about the whole arrangement seemed unnatural, and I wanted to know a little more before committing myself completely.
“‘May I ask where you live, sir?’
“‘Hampshire. Delightful countryside. The Copper Beeches, five miles beyond Winchester. A lovely district, my dear young lady, and the dearest old country house.’
“‘And what would my duties be, sir? I should like to know.’

“‘One child: a dear little rascal, just six. You should see him killing cockroaches with a slipper! Smack! Smack! Smack! Three dead before you can blink!’ He leaned back, laughing until his eyes disappeared again.
“The child’s pastime startled me, but his father laughed so much that I thought he might be joking.
“‘Then my only responsibility would be looking after this one child?’ I asked.

“‘No, no, not your only duty, not your only duty, my dear young lady!’ he cried. ‘As your own good sense will surely tell you, you would be expected to obey any small requests my wife made, provided they were things a lady could properly do. You see no difficulty with that, eh?’
“‘I should be glad to be useful.’
“‘Exactly. Clothing, for instance. We have our little fancies: eccentric, but kind-hearted. If we asked you to wear a particular dress we supplied, you would indulge that small whim, would you not?’
“‘Yes,’ I replied, considerably surprised by the request.
“‘Or if we asked you to sit here, or there, you would not object?’
“‘No, of course not.’
“‘Or to cut your hair very short before joining us?’
“I scarcely trusted my ears. As you see, Mr. Holmes, my hair is thick and has an unusual chestnut colour, which people have called artistic. I could not imagine sacrificing it so casually.
“‘I am afraid that is quite impossible,’ I replied. He had been watching me eagerly with his small eyes, and I could see his face darken as I spoke.
“‘I fear it is essential,’ he said. ‘A little whim of my wife’s. Ladies’ wishes, madam—you know, ladies’ wishes must be respected. So you will not cut it?’
“‘No, sir. I really cannot,’ I said firmly.

“‘Ah, very well; that settles the matter completely. What a pity, for in other respects you really would have suited us very well. In that case, Miss Stoper, I had better see a few more of your young ladies.’

“Throughout this exchange the manageress had sat busy with her papers, without speaking to either of us. Now she glanced at me with such an annoyed expression that I could not help suspecting my refusal had cost her a handsome commission.
“‘Do you want us to keep your name on our books?’ she asked.
“‘Yes, please, Miss Stoper.’

“‘Really, that seems pointless if you reject excellent offers in this fashion,’ she snapped. ‘You can hardly expect us to work hard to find you another opportunity like this. Good day, Miss Hunter.’ She struck the gong on her desk, and the page showed me out.

“Back at my lodgings, Mr. Holmes, I found a nearly empty cupboard and two or three bills on the table. I began to wonder whether I had been foolish. These people might have odd whims and demand obedience in extraordinary matters, but they were willing to pay for their eccentricities. Few governesses in England earn a hundred pounds a year. And what good was my hair to me? Short hair improves many people; perhaps it would improve me. The next day I suspected I had made a mistake. By the day after, I was certain. I had almost swallowed my pride enough to return to the agency and ask whether the post remained available when the gentleman himself wrote. I have his letter here with me, and I shall read it to you:
“‘The Copper Beeches, near Winchester.

“‘Dear Miss Hunter,—Miss Stoper kindly supplied your address. Have you reconsidered your decision? My wife is most eager for you to come, having been greatly impressed by my description. We will pay thirty pounds a quarter, or a hundred and twenty a year, to compensate for any inconvenience our little fancies cause. They are not very demanding. My wife likes a particular electric-blue shade and would like you to wear a dress of that colour indoors during the morning. There is no need to buy one: we have a dress belonging to my dear daughter Alice, now in Philadelphia, which I believe would fit you perfectly. Sitting in particular places or amusing yourself as we suggest should cause no difficulty. As for your hair, cutting it is certainly a pity. Even in our brief meeting I noticed its beauty. Nevertheless, I must insist on this point and hope the higher salary will compensate for your loss. Your duties towards the child will be light. Please try to come. I shall meet you at Winchester with the dog-cart. Tell me which train you will take. Yours faithfully,
“‘JEPHRO RUCASTLE.’

“That is the letter I have just received, Mr. Holmes, and I have decided to accept the offer. Before taking the final step, however, I thought I should like to lay the whole matter before you for consideration.”
“If your decision is made, Miss Hunter, that settles the question,” Holmes replied, smiling.
“You would not advise me to refuse?”
“I admit it is not a position I would want a sister of mine to seek.”
“What can it all mean, Mr. Holmes?”
“I have no evidence to guide me. Perhaps you have formed an opinion yourself?”

“Well, it seems to me that only one explanation is possible. Mr. Rucastle appeared a very kind and good-natured man. Could his wife be mad, and could he want to conceal the fact for fear she would be sent to an asylum, indulging her every fancy to prevent an outburst?”
“That is a possible explanation—indeed, with the information we have, the most likely one. In any event, though, it hardly sounds a pleasant household for a young woman.”
“But the money, Mr. Holmes! The money!”

“Well, yes, the salary is certainly generous—too generous. That is what troubles me. Why pay you a hundred and twenty pounds a year when forty would give them their choice? There must be a powerful reason behind it.”
“I thought that if I explained everything now, you would understand later if I needed help. Knowing you were behind me would give me so much more courage.”

“You can certainly leave here with that assurance. Your little problem promises to be the most interesting that has come my way for several months. Some of its features are distinctly original. If you find yourself uncertain or in danger—”
“Danger! What sort of danger do you expect?”
Holmes shook his head seriously. “If we could define it, it would cease to be dangerous. But whenever you need me, day or night, a telegram will bring me to your assistance.”

“That is all I need.” She rose promptly, anxiety gone from her face. “I can go to Hampshire with an easy mind now. I shall write to Mr. Rucastle immediately, sacrifice my poor hair tonight, and leave for Winchester tomorrow.” After thanking Holmes, she wished us both good night and hurried away.
“At least,” I said, as we heard her quick, firm footsteps going down the stairs, “she seems a young woman quite capable of taking care of herself.”
“She will need to be,” Holmes replied gravely. “Unless I am badly mistaken, we shall hear from her again within a few days.”

It was not very long before my friend’s prediction proved correct. Two weeks passed, and I often found my thoughts turning towards her, wondering what strange corner of human experience this solitary woman had entered. The exceptional salary, peculiar demands, and light workload all suggested something abnormal. Whether it was a whim or a scheme, whether the employer was a benefactor or a villain, I could not decide. Holmes often sat for half an hour at a stretch looking distant and frowning. But whenever I mentioned the matter, he waved it aside. ‘Facts! Facts! Facts!’ he exclaimed impatiently. ‘I cannot make bricks without clay.’ Yet he always ended by muttering that no sister of his should ever have taken such a post.

The telegram finally arrived late one night, just as I was thinking of going to bed and Holmes was settling down to one of his frequent all-night chemical investigations. On such nights I would leave him bent over a retort and a test tube, and find him in the same position when I came down for breakfast. He opened the yellow envelope, glanced at the message and tossed it across to me.
“Look up the trains in Bradshaw,” he said, returning to his chemical work.
The message was short and urgent.
“Please meet me at the Black Swan Hotel, Winchester, at noon tomorrow. Do come! I do not know what to do.
“HUNTER.”
“Will you accompany me?” Holmes asked, looking up.
“I would like to.”
“Then find the train.”
“One leaves at half-past nine,” I said, consulting Bradshaw. “It reaches Winchester at half-past eleven.”
“That will suit us perfectly. Perhaps I should put off my acetone analysis. We may need all our powers tomorrow morning.”

By eleven o’clock the following day we were well on our way to England’s old capital. Holmes had remained absorbed in the morning newspapers throughout the journey, but once we crossed the Hampshire border he threw them down and began admiring the scenery. It was a perfect spring day, with a light blue sky dotted by small, fleecy white clouds drifting from west to east. The sun shone brilliantly, yet an invigorating chill in the air gave a keen edge to one’s energy. All across the countryside, towards the rolling hills around Aldershot, small red and grey farm roofs peeped through the light green of the new leaves.
“How fresh and beautiful they look!” I exclaimed with the enthusiasm of a man newly escaped from Baker Street’s fog.
Holmes, however, shook his head solemnly.

“Do you know, Watson,” he said, “one curse of a mind of my particular kind is that I must view everything in relation to my own special subject? You look at those scattered houses and are struck by their beauty. I look at them and can think only of their isolation, and how crimes might be committed there without fear of punishment.”
“Good heavens!” I cried. “Who would connect these charming old farmhouses with crime?”

“They always fill me with a certain dread. I believe, on the strength of my experience, Watson, that the lowest and vilest alleys of London have no more dreadful record of wickedness than this beautiful, smiling countryside.”
“That is a horrible thought!”

“But the reason is perfectly plain. In a town, the pressure of public opinion can achieve what the law cannot. Even in the vilest alley, the scream of a tortured child or the thud of a drunkard’s blow arouses sympathy and outrage among the neighbours. And the whole machinery of justice is so close that a single complaint can set it in motion: there is only a step from the crime to the dock. Now look at these lonely houses, each standing in its own fields, mostly occupied by poor, ignorant people who know little about the law. Think of the acts of hellish cruelty, the hidden wickedness, that could continue year after year in such places, with no one any the wiser. Had the lady seeking our help gone to live in Winchester, I should never have feared for her. Those five miles of countryside create the danger. Still, it is clear that she is not personally threatened.”
“No. If she can meet us in Winchester, she can leave the house.”
“Exactly. She remains free to go.”
“Then what _can_ be wrong? Can you offer no explanation?”

“I have devised seven separate explanations, each of which fits the facts as far as we know them. But only the fresh information that doubtless awaits us can establish which is correct. Well, there is the cathedral tower, and we shall soon hear everything Miss Hunter has to tell us.”
The Black Swan is a well-regarded inn in the High Street, not far from the station. There we found the young woman waiting for us. She had hired a sitting-room, and our lunch was ready on the table.
“I am so glad you came,” she said earnestly. “It is very kind of you both. Truly, I do not know what to do. Your advice will be invaluable.”
“Please tell us what has been happening.”
“I will, and quickly: I promised to return before three. Mr. Rucastle allowed me to come into town this morning, though he had no idea why I wanted to.”
“Let us hear everything in its proper order.” Holmes stretched his long, thin legs towards the fire and settled down to listen.

“First of all, I should say that, on the whole, I have suffered no actual ill-treatment from Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle. It is only fair to acknowledge that. But I cannot understand them, and I feel uneasy about them.”
“What is it that you cannot understand?”

“Their reasons for behaving as they do. But I shall tell you everything just as it happened. When I arrived, Mr. Rucastle met me here and drove me in his dog-cart to the Copper Beeches. As he said, it is beautifully situated, though the house itself is not beautiful: a large, square, whitewashed building, stained and streaked by damp and bad weather. It stands in its own grounds, with woods on three sides and, on the fourth, a field sloping down to the Southampton high road, which curves past about a hundred yards from the front door. This land in front belongs to the house, but the surrounding woods are part of Lord Southerton’s game preserves. A clump of copper beeches immediately outside the hall door gives the place its name.

“My employer was as pleasant as ever during the drive, and that evening he introduced me to his wife and child. The explanation we thought probable in your rooms at Baker Street was quite wrong, Mr. Holmes. Mrs. Rucastle is not mad. I found her a quiet, pale-faced woman, much younger than her husband. I should judge her no more than thirty, while he can scarcely be under forty-five. From their conversation I gathered that they have been married about seven years; that he was a widower; and that his only child by his first wife was the daughter who has gone to Philadelphia. Mr. Rucastle told me privately that she had left because she had an unreasonable dislike of her stepmother. As the daughter must have been at least twenty, I can readily imagine that living with her father’s young wife had been uncomfortable for her.

“Mrs. Rucastle seemed as colourless in mind as in appearance. She made neither a favourable nor an unfavourable impression on me; she had no presence at all. It was plain that she was passionately devoted to both her husband and her little son. Her pale grey eyes moved constantly between them, noticing every small need and, whenever possible, anticipating it. He too was kind to her, in his blunt, boisterous way, and on the whole they seemed a happy couple. Yet this woman had some secret sorrow. She would often fall into deep thought, with the saddest expression on her face. More than once I have come upon her in tears. I have sometimes thought her child’s nature was weighing on her mind, for I have never known such an utterly spoiled and ill-tempered little creature. He is small for his age, with a disproportionately large head. His entire life seems to alternate between savage fits of rage and dark spells of sulking. His sole idea of amusement seems to be hurting any creature weaker than himself, and he shows remarkable ingenuity in devising ways to catch mice, small birds and insects. But I would rather not speak of the creature, Mr. Holmes; indeed, he has little to do with my story.”
“I welcome every detail,” my friend observed, “whether or not it seems relevant to you.”

“I shall try not to leave out anything important. One unpleasant feature of the house struck me immediately: the servants’ appearance and behaviour. There are only two, a man and his wife. Toller, as he is called, is a rough, uncouth man, with greying hair and whiskers and a constant smell of drink. Twice since my arrival he has been thoroughly drunk, yet Mr. Rucastle appeared not to notice. His wife is very tall and strong, with a sour face. She is as silent as Mrs. Rucastle and much less pleasant. They are a most disagreeable couple, but fortunately I spend most of my time in the nursery and my own bedroom, which stand next to each other in one corner of the house.
“For the first two days after I reached the Copper Beeches, my life was very quiet. On the third, just after breakfast, Mrs. Rucastle came downstairs and whispered something to her husband.

“‘Oh, yes,’ he said, turning to me. ‘We are very grateful to you, Miss Hunter, for indulging our whims to the extent of cutting your hair. I assure you that it has not harmed your appearance in the slightest. Now we shall see how the electric-blue dress suits you. You will find it laid out on the bed in your room, and we should both be extremely grateful if you would be kind enough to put it on.’

“The dress waiting for me was an unusual shade of blue. The material was excellent, a kind of beige fabric, but it showed unmistakable signs of previous wear. It could not have fitted better if it had been made to my measurements. Both Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle expressed delight at its appearance with an enthusiasm that seemed quite excessive. They were waiting in the drawing-room, a very large room running along the whole front of the house, with three long windows extending down to the floor. A chair stood close to the middle window, with its back towards the glass. They asked me to sit there. Then Mr. Rucastle, pacing the other side of the room, began telling some of the funniest stories I have ever heard. You cannot imagine how comical he was; I laughed until I was quite exhausted. Mrs. Rucastle, however, evidently has no sense of humour. She did not even smile, but sat with her hands in her lap and a sad, anxious expression. After an hour or so, Mr. Rucastle suddenly said it was time to begin the day’s duties, and that I could change my dress and join little Edward in the nursery.

“Two days later we repeated the performance in exactly the same circumstances. Once again I changed my dress, sat by the window and laughed heartily at the amusing stories of which my employer possessed an immense store, and which he told with unequalled skill. Then he handed me a yellow-backed novel and moved my chair a little sideways, so that my own shadow would not fall across the page. He asked me to read aloud to him. I read for about ten minutes, starting in the middle of a chapter. Then, abruptly, in the middle of a sentence, he ordered me to stop and change my dress.

“You can easily imagine, Mr. Holmes, how curious I became about the meaning of this extraordinary performance. I noticed that they always took great care to keep my face turned away from the window, until I was consumed by a desire to see what was happening behind me. At first this seemed impossible, but I soon found a way. My hand-mirror had broken, and a happy thought struck me: I concealed a piece of its glass in my handkerchief. On the next occasion, while I was laughing, I raised my handkerchief to my eyes and, with a little adjustment, could see everything behind me. I confess I was disappointed. There was nothing there. At least, that was my first impression. At a second glance, however, I saw a man standing in the Southampton Road—a small, bearded man in a grey suit, who seemed to be looking towards me. It is a busy main road, with people usually passing along it. This man, however, was leaning against the railings bordering our field and looking intently up at the house. I lowered my handkerchief and glanced at Mrs. Rucastle. Her eyes were fixed on me in a most searching stare. She said nothing, but I am convinced she had guessed that I held a mirror and had seen what was behind me. She got up at once.
“‘Jephro,’ she said, ‘there is an impertinent man out on the road, staring up at Miss Hunter.’
“‘He is not a friend of yours, Miss Hunter?’ he asked.
“‘No, I do not know anyone in this neighbourhood.’
“‘Dear me! How very rude! Please turn round and gesture to him to go away.’
“‘Surely it would be better to ignore him altogether?’
“‘No, no; then he would always be hanging about here. Please turn round and wave him away, like this.’

“I obeyed, and at that very moment Mrs. Rucastle pulled down the blind. This was a week ago. Since then I have neither sat by the window again nor worn the blue dress, and I have not seen the man in the road.”
“Please go on,” said Holmes. “Your account promises to be extremely interesting.”

“I am afraid you will find it rather disconnected, and there may turn out to be little connection between the separate incidents I describe. On my very first day at the Copper Beeches, Mr. Rucastle took me to a small outbuilding near the kitchen door. As we approached, I heard the sharp rattle of a chain and what sounded like a large animal moving about inside.
“‘Look in here!’ said Mr. Rucastle, pointing out a gap between two planks. ‘Isn’t he a beauty?’
“I peered through and made out two glowing eyes and an indistinct shape huddled in the darkness.

“‘Don’t be afraid,’ my employer said, laughing at the way I had started. ‘It is only Carlo, my mastiff. I call him mine, but old Toller, my groom, is really the only man who can manage him. We feed him once a day, and not too much even then, so he is always as keen as mustard. Toller turns him loose every night, and God help any trespasser he sinks his teeth into. For goodness’ sake, never step outside after dark on any pretext whatever: your very life would be at risk.’

“The warning was no empty one. Two nights later I happened to look out of my bedroom window at about two in the morning. It was a beautiful moonlit night; the lawn before the house shone silver, almost as bright as day. I stood absorbed in the peaceful beauty of the scene when I noticed something moving in the shadow of the copper beeches. As it came into the moonlight, I saw what it was. A gigantic dog, as large as a calf, with a tawny coat, hanging jowls, black muzzle and enormous protruding bones. It walked slowly across the lawn and disappeared into the shadows on the other side. That dreadful guard chilled my heart in a way I do not think any burglar could have done.

“Now I must tell you of a very strange experience. As you know, I had cut off my hair in London and placed it in a large coil at the bottom of my trunk. One evening, after the child had gone to bed, I amused myself by examining the furniture in my room and rearranging my few possessions. There was an old chest of drawers: the two upper drawers were empty and open, but the bottom one was locked. I had filled the first two with my linen, and as I still had many things to put away, I was naturally annoyed at being unable to use the third. It occurred to me that it might have been locked by mistake, so I took out my bunch of keys and tried to open it. The very first key fitted perfectly, and I pulled the drawer open. It contained only one thing, but I am certain you would never guess what that was. It was my coil of hair.

“I picked it up and examined it. It had the same unusual colour and the same thickness. Then the impossibility of it struck me. How could my hair have been locked inside that drawer? With trembling hands I opened my trunk, emptied it and took my own hair from the bottom. I laid the two locks side by side, and I assure you they were identical. Was it not extraordinary? However much I puzzled over it, I could make nothing of its meaning. I put the strange hair back into the drawer and said nothing to the Rucastles, feeling that I had put myself in the wrong by opening a drawer they had locked.

“I am naturally observant, as you may have noticed, Mr. Holmes, and I soon had a fairly accurate plan of the whole house in my mind. One wing, however, appeared entirely unoccupied. Its entrance faced the door to the Tollers’ quarters, but it was always locked. One day, as I came upstairs, I met Mr. Rucastle coming out of this door with his keys in his hand. His expression made him quite a different person from the round, jovial man I knew. His cheeks were red, his forehead wrinkled with anger, and the veins at his temples bulged with passion. He locked the door and hurried past without a word or a glance at me.

“This aroused my curiosity. When I took the child for a walk in the grounds, I went round to the side where I could see the windows in this part of the house. There were four in a row: three merely dirty, while the fourth was shuttered. They were evidently all deserted. As I walked up and down, occasionally glancing at them, Mr. Rucastle came out to join me, looking as cheerful and jovial as ever.
“‘Ah!’ he said. ‘You must not think me rude for passing without a word, my dear young lady. My mind was occupied with business.’
“I assured him I had taken no offence. ‘By the way,’ I said, ‘you seem to have quite a number of spare rooms up there, and one has its shutters closed.’
“He seemed surprised and, I thought, a little startled by my observation.

“‘Photography is one of my hobbies,’ he said. ‘I have set up my darkroom there. But dear me! What an observant young lady we have found! Who would have thought it? Who could ever have thought it?’ His tone was joking, but there was no joke in his eyes as he looked at me. I could read suspicion and annoyance there, but no amusement.

“Well, Mr. Holmes, from the moment I realised there was something about those rooms that I was not supposed to know, I burned to explore them. It was not simply curiosity, though I have my share of that. It was more a sense of duty—a feeling that some good might come from finding my way inside. People speak of women’s instinct; perhaps that was what gave me the feeling. Whatever it was, I felt it, and I watched eagerly for any opportunity to go through the forbidden door.

“The opportunity came only yesterday. I should tell you that, besides Mr. Rucastle, both Toller and his wife have some business in these deserted rooms. Once I saw Toller carrying a large black linen bag through the door. Lately he has been drinking heavily, and yesterday evening he was very drunk. When I came upstairs, the key was in the door. I have no doubt whatever that he had left it there. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle were both downstairs, with the child, so I had an excellent opportunity. I quietly turned the key in the lock, opened the door and slipped inside.

“Ahead of me was a short passage, with neither wallpaper nor carpet, turning at a right angle at the far end. Around the corner stood three doors in a row, the first and third open. Each led into an empty, dusty, cheerless room, one with two windows and the other with one. The glass was so dirty that the evening light barely glimmered through. The middle door was closed. Across its outside someone had fixed a broad bar from an iron bed, padlocked at one end to a ring in the wall and secured at the other with strong cord. The door itself was locked too, and there was no key. This barricaded door clearly matched the shuttered window outside, yet the gleam beneath it showed that the room was not dark. Evidently a skylight admitted light from above. As I stood in the passage, staring at that sinister door and wondering what secret it concealed, I suddenly heard footsteps inside and saw a shadow passing back and forth across the narrow strip of dim light beneath the door. A wild, irrational terror overwhelmed me, Mr. Holmes. My strained nerves suddenly gave way. I turned and ran—ran as though some dreadful hand were reaching from behind to clutch the skirt of my dress. I rushed along the passage, through the door and straight into the arms of Mr. Rucastle, who was waiting outside.
“‘So,’ he said with a smile, ‘it was you after all. I thought it must be when I saw the open door.’
“‘Oh, I am terribly frightened!’ I gasped.
“‘My dear young lady! My dear young lady!’ You cannot imagine how gentle and soothing his manner was. ‘And what has frightened you, my dear young lady?’
“But his voice was a little too persuasive. He overplayed the kindness, and I was very much on my guard.
“‘I was foolish enough to enter the empty wing,’ I replied. ‘But it is so lonely and eerie in this faint light that I grew frightened and ran out again. Oh, it is so dreadfully quiet in there!’
“‘Nothing more than that?’ he asked, studying me intently.
“‘Why, what else did you imagine?’ I asked.
“‘Why do you suppose I keep this door locked?’
“‘I am quite sure I do not know.’
“‘To keep out people who have no business inside. Do you understand?’ He was still smiling with the greatest apparent good nature.
“‘I am sure that if I had known—’

“‘Well, now you do know. And if you ever step across that threshold again’—in an instant his smile hardened into a furious grin, and he glared down at me with a demon’s face—‘I shall throw you to the mastiff.’

“I was so terrified that I cannot say what I did. I suppose I rushed past him to my room. I remember nothing until I found myself lying on my bed, shaking all over. Then I thought of you, Mr. Holmes. I could not remain there any longer without advice. I feared the house, the man, the woman, the servants—even the child. Every one of them horrified me. If only I could bring you down, everything would be well. Of course I could have fled the house, but my curiosity was almost as powerful as my fear. I soon decided what to do: I would send you a telegram. I put on my hat and cloak, walked to the office, about half a mile from the house, and returned feeling much more at ease. As I approached the door, a dreadful doubt struck me: might the dog be loose? Then I remembered that Toller had drunk himself unconscious that evening. I knew he was the only person in the household who had any influence over the savage creature or would dare release it. I slipped safely inside and lay awake half the night, delighted at the prospect of seeing you. I easily obtained leave to come to Winchester this morning, but I must return before three. Mr. and Mrs. Rucastle are going visiting and will be out all evening, so I must look after the child. Now you have heard all my adventures, Mr. Holmes. I should be very grateful if you could tell me what it all means and, above all, what I ought to do.”
Holmes and I had listened, spellbound, to this extraordinary account. My friend now rose and paced the room with his hands in his pockets and an expression of the deepest seriousness on his face.
“Is Toller still drunk at present?” he asked.
“Yes. I heard his wife telling Mrs. Rucastle that she could do nothing with him.”
“That is good. And the Rucastles are going out tonight?”
“Yes.”
“Is there a cellar with a sound, strong lock?”
“Yes, there is the wine-cellar.”

“Miss Hunter, it seems to me that you have behaved with great courage and good sense throughout this affair. Could you manage one more difficult task? I should not ask it if I did not consider you a quite exceptional woman.”
“I shall try. What must I do?”

“My friend and I shall reach the Copper Beeches by seven o’clock. The Rucastles will have left by then, and we hope Toller will still be helpless. That leaves only Mrs. Toller, who might raise the alarm. If you could send her into the cellar on an errand and then lock her in, you would make our task very much easier.”
“I shall do it.”

“Excellent! Then we shall investigate the affair thoroughly. There is, of course, only one plausible explanation. You have been brought there to impersonate someone, and the real person is being held prisoner in that room. That much is obvious. As for the prisoner’s identity, I have no doubt she is the daughter—Miss Alice Rucastle, if I remember correctly—who was said to have gone to America. They undoubtedly chose you because you resemble her in height, build and hair colour. Her hair had been cut off, very possibly during some illness she had suffered, so naturally yours had to be sacrificed as well. By a curious chance, you discovered her hair. The man in the road was certainly a friend of hers, possibly her fiancé. Since you wore her dress and looked so much like her, your laughter whenever he saw you, followed by your gesture, doubtless convinced him that Miss Rucastle was perfectly happy and no longer wanted his attentions. The dog is released at night to prevent him from attempting to communicate with her. All that is fairly clear. The gravest aspect of the case is the child’s character.”
“What on earth does that have to do with it?” I exclaimed.

“My dear Watson, as a doctor you continually learn about a child’s tendencies by studying its parents. Do you not see that the reverse is equally valid? I have often gained my first real understanding of parents’ characters by observing their children. This child is abnormally cruel, simply for the pleasure of cruelty. Whether he inherits this from his smiling father, as I suspect, or from his mother, it is an ominous sign for the poor girl in their power.”

“I am certain you are right, Mr. Holmes!” our client cried. “A thousand things return to my mind that convince me you have found the truth. Oh, let us not lose a moment in helping this poor creature.”
“We must proceed cautiously: we are dealing with a very cunning man. We can do nothing before seven o’clock. We shall be with you then, and it will not take us long to solve the mystery.”

We kept our promise. It was precisely seven when we reached the Copper Beeches, after leaving our carriage at a roadside public-house. Even if Miss Hunter had not stood smiling on the doorstep, the group of trees would have identified the house, their dark leaves gleaming like polished metal in the setting sun.
“Have you managed what we discussed?” Holmes asked.
A loud thumping came from somewhere below. “That is Mrs. Toller in the cellar,” she said. “Her husband is lying on the kitchen rug, snoring. Here are his keys: they are duplicates of Mr. Rucastle’s.”
“You have done extremely well!” Holmes exclaimed enthusiastically. “Now show us the way, and we shall soon get to the bottom of this wicked business.”

We climbed the stairs, unlocked the door and followed the passage until we stood before the barricade Miss Hunter had described. Holmes cut the cord and took away the bar across the door. He tried the various keys in the lock, but none fitted. There was no sound from inside. At this silence his expression darkened.
“I hope we have not arrived too late,” he said. “Miss Hunter, I think we had better enter without you. Now, Watson, put your shoulder against it, and let us see whether we can force our way inside.”

The old, unsteady door yielded at once to our combined strength. We rushed into the room together. It was empty. Its only furniture was a small pallet bed, a little table and a basket of linen. The skylight overhead stood open, and the prisoner had gone.
“Some villainy has taken place here,” said Holmes. “This fine fellow has guessed Miss Hunter’s intentions and carried his victim away.”
“But by what means?”

“Through the skylight. We shall soon discover how he did it.” He swung himself onto the roof. “Ah, yes!” he called. “Here is the end of a long, light ladder against the eaves. That explains how he managed it.”
“But that is impossible,” said Miss Hunter. “The ladder was not there when the Rucastles left.”

“He has returned and done it. I tell you, he is a clever and dangerous man. I should not be at all surprised if those footsteps I hear on the stairs belong to him. Watson, I think you would do well to have your pistol ready.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when a man appeared in the doorway: a very fat, powerfully built man carrying a heavy stick. At the sight of him Miss Hunter screamed and shrank against the wall, but Sherlock Holmes sprang forward to confront him.
“You scoundrel!” he demanded. “Where is your daughter?”
The fat man glanced around the room, then up towards the open skylight.

“I should be asking you that!” he shrieked. “You thieves! Spies and thieves! So I have caught you, have I? You are in my power. I shall deal with you!” He turned and clattered downstairs as fast as he could.
“He has gone to fetch the dog!” Miss Hunter cried.
“I have my revolver with me,” I said.

“We had better close the front door!” Holmes cried, and we all rushed downstairs together. We had scarcely reached the hall when we heard a hound baying, followed by a scream of agony and a horrible sound of savage tearing that was dreadful to hear. An elderly, red-faced man, his limbs shaking, staggered out through a side door.
“My God!” he cried. “Someone has let the dog loose. It has had no food for two days. Quickly, quickly, or we shall be too late!”

Holmes and I rushed outside and round the corner of the house, with Toller hurrying after us. The enormous, starving beast had buried its black muzzle in Rucastle’s throat as he writhed and screamed on the ground. I ran up and shot it through the head. It toppled over, its sharp white teeth still locked in the deep folds of his neck. With great difficulty we pulled them apart and carried him indoors, alive but horribly torn. We laid him on the drawing-room sofa. After sending the now sober Toller to take the news to his wife, I did what I could to ease his pain. We were all gathered around him when the door opened and a tall, gaunt woman came in.
“Why, Mrs. Toller!” Miss Hunter exclaimed.
“Yes, miss. Mr. Rucastle released me when he returned, before he went upstairs to you. Ah, miss, it is a pity you never told me your plans. I could have told you that you were wasting your trouble.”
“Ha!” said Holmes, examining her closely. “Clearly Mrs. Toller knows more about this affair than any of us.”
“Yes, sir, I do, and I am quite willing to tell you what I know.”
“Then please sit down and let us hear it. There are several points, I must confess, about which I am still completely in the dark.”

“I shall soon explain it to you,” she said. “I would have done so before now if I could have got out of the cellar. If this leads to a case in the police court, remember that I was your friend, and Miss Alice’s friend as well.

“Miss Alice was never happy at home after her father married again. They treated her as though she did not matter and gave her no say in anything. But things did not become really bad until she met Mr. Fowler at a friend’s house. As far as I could learn, a will gave Miss Alice rights to money of her own. But she was so quiet and patient that she never said anything about them and simply left everything in Mr. Rucastle’s hands. He knew he was safe with her. When there was a prospect of a husband who would demand everything the law entitled him to, her father decided it was time to put a stop to it. He wanted her to sign a document allowing him to use her money whether or not she married. When she refused, he kept tormenting her until she developed brain-fever and lay close to death for six weeks. At last she recovered, worn to a shadow, with her beautiful hair cut off. But that made no difference to her young man: he remained as faithful to her as any man could be.”
“Ah,” said Holmes, “I think your account makes the affair fairly clear, and I can work out the rest. Mr. Rucastle then began, I presume, keeping her imprisoned in this way?”
“Yes, sir.”
“And he brought Miss Hunter from London to put an end to Mr. Fowler’s unwelcome persistence.”
“That is exactly right, sir.”

“But Mr. Fowler, being a persistent man, as a good sailor ought to be, kept the house under siege. On meeting you, he managed through certain arguments—whether in the form of coins or otherwise—to persuade you that your interests matched his.”
“Mr. Fowler was a very kindly spoken and generous gentleman,” Mrs. Toller replied calmly.
“And by this means he ensured that your husband had no shortage of drink, and that a ladder would be ready the moment your master left the house.”
“You have it exactly as it happened, sir.”

“I am sure we owe you an apology, Mrs. Toller,” said Holmes. “You have certainly explained everything that puzzled us. Here come the country surgeon and Mrs. Rucastle, so I think, Watson, we had better escort Miss Hunter back to Winchester. Our standing in this matter now seems rather questionable to me.”

And so we solved the mystery of the sinister house with the copper beeches outside its door. Mr. Rucastle survived, but remained a broken man, kept alive only by his devoted wife’s care. They still live with their old servants, who probably know so much about Rucastle’s past that he finds it difficult to dismiss them. Mr. Fowler and Miss Rucastle married by special licence in Southampton the day after their escape. He now holds a government appointment on the island of Mauritius. As for Miss Violet Hunter, I was rather disappointed that my friend Holmes showed no further interest in her once she was no longer at the centre of one of his problems. She is now head of a private school at Walsall, where, I believe, she has enjoyed considerable success.
